I have the honour to inform the house that I have received the following letter:
Ottawa, April 20, 1934.
Sir,-I have the honour to inform you that Right Hon. Sir Lyman P. Duff, acting as the deputy of His Excellency the Governor General, will proceed to the Senate chamber to-day at 5 p.m. for the purpose of giving the royal assent to certain bills.
F. L. C. Pereira,
Deputy Assistant Secretary
to the Governor General.

Mr. A. U. G. BURY (East Edmonton) presented the third report of the select standing committee on standing orders and moved that the report be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.
On the orders of the day.

On the first reading of the sweepstakes bill the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) suggested that the government might fix a certain day for discussion of the matter. Is it the present intention that the bill will be proceeded with this evening or shall we take up public bills in the ordinary course?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I thank the hon. gentleman for directing attention to the matter. It is proposed to suit the convenience of all members of the house in fixing a day for discussion of the sweepstakes bill, possibly some day next week. The Secretary of State will lay on the table as soon as he can have it prepared, a copy of the resolution that was passed by the legislative assembly of Quebec and a copy of the bill that was passed at the last session of the assembly. I think that can probably be done on Monday. Then we can fix some convenient day for the discussion of the sweepstakes bill after consultation with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and others who may be interested.

WASHOUT AT MATAPEDIA, BONAVENTURE COUNT?
On the orders of the day:

I would call the attention of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) to a Canadian Press dispatch appearing in this morning's papers concerning a very serious interruption to traffic on the main line of the Canadian National Railways in Matapedia in my county, where passengers, baggage and mail have had to be transferred by canoe over the Resti-gouche river. Owing to the very heavy fall of snow in the Matapedia valley during the past winter there has been a washout of several hundred yards of the main line, and trains have been held up three or four at a time. I have been urging for many years the erection of protection works for the main line and village of Matapedia and I hope that with this occurrence the Minister of Railways will take a deeper interest in the
P. E. I. Car Ferry

matter. In the meantime I would ask if he has any further information beyond what has appeared in this morning's papers?

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext: The hon. gentleman sent a request over to my office for information, and I have a good deal of information here which I will send across to him. It is not of particular interest to the rest of the house. I may say in a sentence-

I wish the minister would give the information to the house so that it will appear in Hansard because my people are deeply interested in it. In Gloucester county we are almost cut off from communication with northern New Brunswick.

I was going to say that the railway informs me that they have complete control of the matter and are taking every procedure needed. I thought it would be sufficient if I said that and sent the letter across to my hon. friend from Bonaventure and anybody else who wants to see it.
On the orders of the day:

I would ask the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) if there is any truth in the newspaper report that the radio broadcasting station at Windsor is being taken over by the radio commission for a period of five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I will look into the matter and give my hon. friend the information.
On the orders of the day:

I wish to
direct the attention of the Minister of Railways to an editorial that appeared in the Charlottetown Guardian of April 16 in which it is stated that the government of Prince Edward Island had taken up with the railway trustee board the matter of rates charged for automobiles on the car ferry and that they had been referred to Mr. Allison Fraser, being informed that he was the man who had authority in this regard. The editorial states that Mr. Fraser has refused to put into force this year the rates that were in force last year during the tourist season. May I say to the Minister of Railways that we as a province absolutely refuse to accept Mr. Fraser's dictum in this matter, and I trust that the Minister of Railways will look into

the subject with a view to seeing that our province receives at least the same rates as were in force last year.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways) :
speechtext:
The statement is correct in so far
as it indicates that the government of Prince Edward Island had seen the officials of the railway, but I may inform the hon. gentleman that they also interviewed myself some months ago. A deputation from Prince Edward Island saw me and I have had the matter up for some time with the railway management; but inasmuch as the car ferry is in a sense operated separately from the railways, it was a matter in which the government had a right to have a fairly strong opinion in regard to rates. My own opinion, passed on to the management-and I believe they are accepting it-was that the wisest course would be to observe exactly the same rates as were in force last year in connection with the tourist traffic. If they do, I fancy that will be satisfactory, though I may add that there are some people in the province who protest that there should be even lower rates than last year. The best that can be hoped for, however, is that during the tourist season there will be charged the same rates as were in effect last year.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, Aprjl 19, consideration of the motion of Mr. Weir (Melfort) for the second reading of Bill No. 51, to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provisions in connection therewith, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
In rising
to speak to the amendment proposed by the leader of the opposition to this bill, may I at the outset extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and to the group he leads upon the outstanding success they have had in winning over the Prime Minister and the government to the wholehearted adoption of their policy. For if this bill is carried into effect it will involve in the agricultural industry, in the mining industry, in the fishing industry and in many of our manufacturing industries a complete system of planned and regulated economy from the primary producer right through to the consumer. The hon. member for Winnipeg

Marketing Act-Mr. Young
North Centre recognized the situation yesterday when he said that this would probably result in a realignment of political parties in Canada.
We of the Liberal party have always contended that the C.C.F. party and the Conservative party are much closer together in their political philosophy than either one of them is to the Liberal party-

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext: Even that would be to their credit.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext: -and I think the developments of the present session will show that there is much truth in that contention. The government received considerable support for its relief bill from gentlemen in the corner, and now gentlemen in the corner are getting full support for their policy from the government.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext: Quid pro quo.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext: In this connection, might I refer to a statement made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. gentleman that some of us in this corner voted against the relief bill.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
I said considerable support. The statement to which I wish to refer is found on page 2337 of Hansard of yesterday. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said:
I am willing to accept the explanation of the leader of the opposition that there was no implication, but in making that explanation the leader of the opposition says that we are seeking to wipe out parliamentary institutions . . . and it is not true.
I am glad to hear the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre make that denial, but I attended the convention of the C.C.F. in Regina last summer, and for three days I sat in the gallery listening to the debates that took place there. Many startling statements were made but I took down what I considered to be the most startling, which was made by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Maclnnis). They were discussing whether or not they should proceed by constitutional means to take over the government of the country and the hon. gentleman argued that they should proceed by constitutional means because, he said, if they were not strong enough to get into power by means of the ballot they were not strong enough to get in by any other means; but, he added, "When we get the power of the state in our hands we will use that power to keep it in our hands." Let us examine that statement. What is the
power of the state? It is the power to make laws and to enforce them, and the proposal made here is that they should first get into power and then make laws that will render it impossible for anyone to turn them out of power again. If that is not depriving parliament of its rights, I do not know what is.
This legislation is based on the assumption that a small group of men, chosen in part by the government and in part in other ways, are more capable of managing the individual businesses of farmers, of lumbermen, of fishermen and of manufacturers in this country than are the men who own the businesses. Under our present system, if I mismanage my business I suffer for it, and that is the incentive to me to keep right up on my toes and attend to business. But under this legislation it is assumed that a group of men who have no direct financial interest in the business will be in a better position to manage it and to put it on a profitable basis than I can myself.
I have little sympathy with those who say that they agree with the principle of the bill but are opposed to the details. To me the whole principle is abhorrent. The very idea of a marketing board sitting here in Ottawa and telling the farmers of the country how many acres of wheat they shall sow, how many acres of oats, how many acres of barley and of flax, how many head of cattle they shall be allowed to raise, how many hogs they shall fatten, how many chickens they shall feed, that board having the power to put them in gaol if they dare to sell any of these in violation of its ruling-why, the whole idea is abhorrent to anyone of Liberal thought. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) the other day, speaking to the bill, made this statement: "The principle behind the bill is that the producer should have in his own hand the power to control the marketing of his own products." That is not the principle of the bill; that is the very antithesis of its principle. The principle of the bill is that the power should be taken out of the hands of the producer to control his own product. I was surprised, I was shocked the other day, when the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Bradette) was speaking, at an interruption made by the Prime Minister. The hon. member was speaking against the curtailment of the rights of the people and the Prime Minister made the statement that "All legislation restricts liberty; that that is what parliament is for." That is not what parliament is for. Parliament was set up in the first place and has been maintained through the ages to protect and maintain the rights and liberties of the people against those who would encroach upon them.
Marketing Act-Mr. Young

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
And protection has
always meant restriction. If the hon. member would read a little history he would know that.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
If every law that is passed
restricts liberty to some extent, that is no reason that we should pass a law restricting all liberty. If every law that is passed means a restriction of liberty, we should be all the more careful what laws we do pass and this one should certainly never be passed.
Last night, discussing what he called the necessity for the bill, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) referred to quotas set up by different countries of the world restricting the imports of various commodities allowed into those countries. He instanced that as one of the reasons which made this bill necessary. There is nothing in this legislation to overcome that difficulty. I realize fully the difficulty of carrying on international trade in the present temper of the world, but in this bill there is nothing to solve that problem. In some quarters a very mistaken idea exists as to the meaning of the granting of a quota. Many people think that when the government of one country grants a quota to another, it means that the country granting the quota undertakes to buy that quantity of goods from the other. That is not the situation. If, for instance, Great Britain gives us a quota of a million barrels of apples a year, that does not mean that she will buy a million barrels from us; it means that the British government says to us: We will permit you to ship a million barrels into our country but you must take your chance of being able to sell them when they get here; you must find your own market after the apples arrive. I ask this question: Will the boards that will be set up under this bill to take care of the marketing of our apples, be any more successful in finding those markets than would be the scores and scores of individuals who are now trying to sell and whose financial interests are at stake if they do not find a market for their goods? If this legislation comes into effect, we shall probably have three local boards in Canada handling apples: one in Nova Scotia, one in Ontario and one in British Columbia.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext: And one in Ottawa.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Yes, a central board in
Ottawa, but it will not do the marketing; it will do only the meddling, so to speak; it will have authority to restrict the powers of those local boards, but it will be the duty of the local boards to find markets for our apples. Will those three local boards be

more successful than the individuals who own the apples and whose financial interests are at stake if they fail to find a market for them? Supposing one board is a little more enterprising than the others and does find a market in some part of the world for a certain quantity of apples: would it be able to supply that market? Not without permission of the central marketing board. What would the central marketing board say to them? It would say: You have done well to find that market but you must share it with the other two boards. So the poor board that has found this market discovers that in order to sell one barrel of apples it has to find a market for three barrels. What incentive would there be then to find any market for their goods? In any case, why should they care? Their salaries and expenses will go on regardless of whether the apples are sold. If the apples are even dumped in the ocean, that will make no difference to the board because their pay will go on just the same. In that event they would be apt simply to settle back into a state of dull routine and let the marketing take care of itself.
The other day I heard a story-and I believe the Minister of Trade and Commerce heard it also-of a board set up in a certain part of the country to handle the raw product of its customers. It was not dependent upon service for its clientele; it had that bound to it by a contract. What happened? There were in the market three principal buyers for the commodity and the board did what? The first week they sold all their receipts to buyer number one; the second week they sold all their receipts to buyer number two; the third week they sold all their receipts to buyer number three; the fourth week they sold all their receipts to buyer number one; the fifth week they sold all their receipts to buyer number two; the sixth week they sold all their receipts to buyer number three; the next week they sold all their receipts to buyer number one, and so on, and they continued that process from one year's end to the other. What had they done? They had ceased to function as a selling agency; they had simply sat back and allowed the business to run itself. Yet that board was under more direct control of the producers than will be the boards that will be set up under this bill.
There is a further danger that those boards might decide to withhold from the market the products they have to sell. People getting into that position, handling large quantities of goods not at their own risk, might think the price ought to go up, but the judgment of the world is that it will not go up, so the world offers a certain price for the commodity.

Marketing Act-Mr. Young
They match their judgment against the judgment of the world and having nothing at stake, they hold back those commodities from the market. There must be a great deal of fun in playing the market in that way. Some people in Canada have had many millions of dollars worth of that kind of fun in recent years and the taxpayers are going to pay for it, but I do not think we want any more experiences of that kind.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) the other night, speaking on the bill, outlined the cause of failure of some of the cooperative associations. He said that one reason was that they were apt to choose as their salesmen, their managers, men who had no direct financial interest in the affairs of the cooperative. That difficulty is not removed by this bill as we shall see when we come to discuss it item by item. Those boards that will have control of the marketing are not directly responsible to the producers. Let us look at the bill itself. Subclause (1) of clause 3 reads:
The governor in council may establish a board' to be known as the dominion marketing board-
This board is not to be appointed by the producers. The dominion marketing board will be appointed by the governor in council. Subclause (2) reads:
The board shall consist of such number of persons as the governor in council may from time to time determine, and each member shall hold office during pleasure and shall receive such remuneration as the governor in council shall determine.
Not elected by the producers; not under their control; not in direct touch with them and not necessarily in sympathy with them. Subclause (4) reads:
The governor in council may authorize certain members of the board to exercise the functions of the board in respect of any product or class of products.
What does that mean? It means that the government will not make the mistake it made in the case of the tariff board. In that case it appointed three men and the chairman happened to be a man who would not jump every time the string was pulled. If any man happens to get on this board who dares to think for himself and who does not agree with the minister, the governor in council may authorize the other members of the board to do all the work and that man will have nothing to do. Subclause (9) of clause 3 reads:
The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purposes of this act.
This board is to have power to use the taxpayers' money to carry on its activities.
The powers of the board are given in clause 4, and among them are the following:
To regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated product that shall be marketed by any person at any time, and to prohibit the marketing of any of the regulated product of any grade or quality.
I wonder whether the government has given consideration to all that is involved in that clause. I know there are in the house some ministers who believe certain classes, that is the lower grades, of cattle should not be marketed. If one of those gentlemen happened to be the man in charge, he would prohibit the marketing of low grade cattle. In that event, consider the position of the farmer in the dried-out district whose crops have failed, whose cattle are thin and who is in no position to fit them for the market. What can he do? The only thing that man can do is to throw his cattle on the market and get what he can for them. But under this legislation it would be impossible, for the board would say: No, we will not allow you to market your lean cattle because it would interfere with the price other men can get for their fat cattle. Then there is the power to prohibit marketing. I wonder if anyone has considered the political possibilities of that clause. Suppose, for instance, the board forbids the export of lumber. An election is about to take place. Some unscrupulous politician comes into a lumber district and says: Boys, if you vote right they are going to open the gates and let us sell lumber again. Is that likely to make any difference to the election? I wonder if the government has given consideration to such a possibility.
Then subsection (c). The board shall have powerto compensate any person for loss sustained by exporting, storing or withholding from the market any product pursuant to any determination or order of the board;
The significance of that clause is that it would guarantee the top price to every one; for those who get the lower price will say to the board: You ordered us to sell in a certain place; someone else who sold in another place got a higher price; now you must compensate us, give us the difference between what we got and what they got. You can pay it out of the treasury. Suppose the price of apples in Canada were $5 a barrel, and suppose it were only $4 a barrel abroad. The board could order the Canadian apple shippers to export large quantities of apples and dump them on the world market at as

Marketing Act-Mr. Young
low as $3 a barrel in order to get rid of them. In so doing they could create an artificial shortage in Canada and force the price up to say $6 a barrel. Then those who had sold abroad at $3 would be able to come back to this board and demand compensation, demand the same remuneration for their apples as received by those who sold at home at $6. So the consumers of this country would be in this position: in the first place they would pay $6 for their own apples, and then would have to pay $2 or $3 a barrel for the apples eaten by the people in other countries.
Then the next clause:
(d)	to compensate any person in respect of any shipment made pursuant to any determination or order of the board to a country whose currency is depreciated, in relation to Canadian currency, for loss due to such depreciation;
That is to say, this board undertakes to guarantee, to back the notes of other countries. In private business it is not considered good business to baek any one else's notes. But here we have a board that can lightly assume the responsibility of backing the notes of foreign countries. That would not be very easy to carry out. If a country with which we are dealing has its currency depreciated 50 per cent in relation to ours that depreciation will be in greater or lesser degree reflected in the number of that country's dollars which will buy our products; those who ship goods to that country will get more of those dollars for them. They will come to the government with these dollars and say: We have got so many of these dollars, but they are not worth par in our dollars; please make an adjustment by giving us good Canadian dollars in exchange for these depreciated dollars of another country.
Then look at the next clause:
(e)	to assist by grant or loan the construction or operation of facilities for preserving, storing, or conditioning the regulated product and to assist research work relating to the marketing of such product;
That is to say, this board will have power to dip into the public treasury and either give or lend money. What for? For the establishment of saw mills, flour mills, bakeries, canning factories, tobacco factories, breweries, distilleries, and to put in charge of them men who perhaps do not know anything about running them. But that will not matter, for they have the public treasury to fall back on, and if they do not know how to do the work they will be furnished with research men to carry on research work so that they can tell them how to conduct their business. I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) in his seat; I will be sorry for him

when this bill takes effect, for there will be very little money in the treasury to balance the budget when these boys get through.
Then in (f) we find the board shall have power:
to require any or all persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product to register their names, addresses and occupations with the board, or to obtain a licence from the board, and such licence shall be subject to cancellation by the board for violation of any provision of this act or regulation made thereunder;
Every person, farmer, lumberman, fisherman, manufacturer, must go to the board every year and get his licence, and that licence will dictate what he shall do and how he shall do it. How easy it would be to withhold the licence of one that you wanted to get out of the way. Withhold the licence of a farmer, his farm would become worthless and someone's friend could buy it at a small price.
Then look at the next clause:
(g) to require full information relating to the production and marketing of the natural product from all persons engaged therein and to require periodic returns to be made by such persons, and inspect the books and premises of such persons;
The idea of appointing men to go out in the farming country and insist on every farmer making returns! Of what? Of everything he had produced and what he sold it for or did with it. The farmer's wife must account for every dozen of eggs that she sold. And all these reports would be sent to Ottawa. Imagine the number of civil servants required to tabulate all this and check it up!
Then the board is to have power:
(j) to cooperate with any marketing board or agency established under the law of any province to regulate the marketing of any natural product of such province and to act conjointly with any such provincial board or agency;
What is that for? In order that the federal and provincial boards can combine their powers and activities to defeat the purposes of the British North America Act. The provisions of the constitution were enacted to protect the rights and property of the citizens. Now those who desire to get control of other people's business and manage it for them sometimes find those provisions awkward, they are in the way. So they devise this scheme to defeat the purposes of the constitution.
Then look at section 5, marketing schemes -a great word:
(1)	A representative number of persons engaged in the production and marketing or the production or marketing of a natural product may petition the governor in council

Marketing Act-Mr. Young
to approve a scheme for the regulation of the marketing of such natural product by a local board under the supervision of the board.
You notice, sir, that it is "the production and marketing or the production or marketing." Under that clause the members of the Winnipeg Grain Exchange could hatch a scheme, present it to the government, and if they had a sympathetic minister they could have that scheme put into effect without the farmers knowing anything about it, and give themselves a monopoly of the grain trade of this country.
(2)	The petition shall be filed with the minister and if he considers that the persons engaged in the production or marketing of the natural product are sufficiently represented by the petitioners, the scheme shall be referred to the board with a request for a report on the expediency thereof.
What number would be a representative number? It just depends on the minister. In our country a township is a block of land six miles square. The minister might take the view that one farmer from each township would be a fairly representative number of the farmers of the west. Is that an extreme case? I know one more extreme. Only three years ago my right hon. friend the Prime Minister went to Regina and met three or four farmers from Saskatchewan who told him a certain thing. He considered that they were representative of the farmers of Saskatchewan, and acted accordingly. " A representative number " is a very wide and elastic term. Perhaps three or four men in the whole province might be considered a representative number. Then the people most concerned, the farmers whose business is going to be taken out of their hands, the lumbermen whose business is going to be controlled by this organization, the fishermen, will know nothing until an announcement appears in the Gazette that this thing is done. And the farmers never see the Gazette.
Let us see how these local boards are to be set up. The first step is that a number of men engaged in a certain industry get together and hatch a scheme, for marketing a certain product. These schemers choose from among themselves a chairman, and they elect a board. Then they draw up a petition which they present to the minister outlining their scheme. They also select a head office, and they say who their chief executive officers are to be. They even make the appointments. They submit all this to the minister and the minister submits it to the board in Ottawa. What does this board in Ottawa know about it? It is quite out of touch with the producers on the farm, the fishermen on the sea, the lumbermen in the forest, but this board shall decide whether or not the scheme
is acceptable. If they decide that it is, the announcement is made in the Gazette, and the producers, the people most concerned, know nothing about it until they are all in, and the schemers are in control. Well, can they get out of the scheme? Yes, there is a way out. How can they get out? They must circulate a petition, but the petition they must circulate to get out is not the same petition they use to get in. Any petition to get in only requires what the minister called a representative number, which may mean three or four people in a province or one person in a township, but in order to get out they must have this sort of petition:
(2)	A representative number of the persons operating under a scheme approved under section 5 of this act may petition the minister to revoke the scheme.
(3)	The petition shall disclose to what extent the persons operating under the scheme are represented by those signing the petition and the minister shall decide whether all those so engaged are sufficiently represented-
The number on the petition to get out is much more comprehensive than the number on the petition to get in. It must represent all those engaged in the industry, and the minister has the right to refuse that petition if he sees fit to do so. Then let us look at section 9, which is the worst of all:
Notwithstanding that no petition in relation to any natural product has been filed, the minister may, if he is satisfied that the trade and commerce in the said' product is injuriously affected by the lack of a local board to regulate such product, at any time propose a scheme for the marketing of such productand so on. The minister may impose a scheme without consulting the people at all. From what I have seen here I have an idea that there are some ministers who hold the opinion that certain classes of people should not be allowed to do business at all and who would, if they had it in their power, shut them out. The minister who is put in charge of this legislation might happen to be one of those so disposed; he might say that certain classes of people are not to be allowed to do business in any particular line, and might hatch a scheme to put them out of business, and that scheme would become law.
Then when we turn to section 12 we find that power is given to over-ride the Customs Act, to restrict imports coming into this country, as though they were not sufficiently restricted already. Not only that, but power is given also to prohibit the export from Canada of any commodity so regulated. What Canada needs most to-day is markets, and every ounce of energy we have available should be devoted to the finding of markets.

Marketing Act-Mr. Young
Yet if any man goes out and finds a market for his product without consulting this board, after having found that market this board can forbid Kim to supply it. What inducement is there for anyone to find markets in order to help dispose of the products of this country? We are asked to surrender all these things to this board, and what do we get in return; what do they offer us in exchange? They offer us the privilege of having our private business taken out of our hands and put into the hands of a bureaucracy that has no financial interest at stake, that probably knows nothing about running the business and that is not in any way hurt if the business fails, but we will have to pay the bills if they make a mess of things.
The other day at the Rome conference France made an offer; they said, "We are willing to buy wheat from you if you are willing to buy something from us." Would not the government be much better advised to find markets like that and say to France, "All right, we are ready to deal with you," instead of trying to regulate the production and marketing of goods in Canada? With this bureaucracy set up and no one else allowed to do business all hope of progress and improvement in this country in marketing and fashioning our goods must die, for there will be no interest on the part of the bureaucracy in making any improvement. They will be secure in their seats; they will not be in the least concerned as to whether or not our products are marketed to the best advantage.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote a few words from the essay on liberty by John Stuart Mill. I wish hon. gentlemen opposite and in the corner would study that work carefully.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAE PRODUCTS
speechtext:
When was it written?
Mr. YrOUNG: It was written long ago; so was the bible.
The only unfailing and permanent source of improvement is liberty, since by it there are as many possible independent centres of improvement as there are individuals. . . . But where everything is done through a bureaucracy, nothing to which the bureaucracy is opposed can be done at all.
And again:
A state that dwarfs its men in order that they may be more docile instruments in its hands, even for beneficial purposes, will find that with small men no great thing can really be accomplished; and that the perfection of machinery to which it has sacrificed everything will in the end avail it nothing, for want of the vital power which, in order that the machine might run more smoothly, it has preferred to banish.
Just in closing I should like to make one more reference. Yesterday the live stock pro-

ducers of western Canada appeared before the price spreads committee. They are opposed to this or any other marketing bill, and for the benefit of the Minister of Agriculture I should like to read what they have to say:
It would seem then that if our departments of agriculture would function as we wish them to, there would be no need for superimposing further expense on the country for a board . . . departments of agriculture appear to be set up to serve governmental policies which may be a vastly different thing from serving the farmers. If departmental officials can function freely with the one objective in view, viz. that of aiding the industry it does not appear necessary to establish any additional board.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not one of those who are very much enamoured of the idea of what may be known as government interference in business. There has been a great deal of it in this country; there may be a great deal more, but at the present moment we are faced not with a theory but with a condition, and sometimes when we are faced with conditions we must give up cherished theories. While, as I say, as a rule I am not in favour of government interference in business, there come times in the history of the world, such as the present, when governments must,-not interfere in business,-but use the powers of government for the purpose of assisting and promoting business.
Yesterday we heard something about restricted markets and restricted production. With the exception of the first two or three speeches during this debate we have heard nothing from hon. gentlemen opposite but an attempt to becloud the real purpose of this bill. There is not a single word in the bill from beginning to end with regard to the restriction of production. The only principle contained in this bill is authority to take measures for the purpose not of restricting markets but of making it possible to market the goods which the farmers and other people in this country are producing.
We have heard a great deal about liberty. Liberty is one of those wonderful things that have come down to us through the ages, but we cannot meet present conditions by the doctrinaire philosophy of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). What the people in this country are up against at the moment is the fact that they have not liberty to handle their products in such a way as to get the best results, and the primary producer in this country wants liberty-not according to John Stuart Mill-but liberty to live and make a decent living out of his production. I should think hon. gentlemen

Marketing Act-Mr. Turnbull
opposite would hang their heads in shame when anyone talks about restricted markets. When they came into power in 1922 our markets were not so very badly restricted; we were selling $200,000,000 worth of farm products annually to the United States, but while the opposition stood by and said they were afraid to pass legislation for the benefit of Canada lest they might provoke the United States, one by one our markets slipped away from us.
Must we place on Hansard again, for perhaps the fiftieth time, the fact that the markets for our wheat were lost during the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite? In 1925 Mussolini started the "battle of the grain," as he called it, and that was five years before this government came into power. That was followed by the imposition of tariffs by Germany, France and Italy, which were among our principal markets for wheat. Are not these gentlemen honest enough to go out and tell the public that the markets of our Canadian farmers were lost during their regime, not because of anything their party did and not because of anything our party did but because foreign countries desired to preserve their own markets for their own people and their own purposes. If their party was responsible at all it was responsible for that attitude which said, "We are not prepared to raise our general tariff, and we are not prepared to increase our British preference lest it might be misunderstood across the border." And then they come back and try to talk to us about restricting markets. There have been no steps taken by this government, since it came into office, which in any way restricted markets. There have been no steps taken by this government since it came into office which have not been for the purpose.of obtaining markets for our natural products. The imperial conference treaties -and hon. members opposite are still throwing slurs at them-have provided markets for many of our natural products, markets which this country would have been very sorry not to have had, and markets which this country would not have had if hon. gentlemen opposite had had their way.

You see it illustrated in the question asked last night by the leader of the opposition when someone said, "If we are going to have orderly marketing we have to have some machinery." He said, "What have we been doing about it all along." That is the attitude of the Liberal party, that what they have been doing all along must be indefinitely continued,-nothing new, nothing to take the place of anything else, but just to let it drift. That is what they did during nine years of office, and that is just exactly what brought this country to the pass it was in in 1930.
The unemployment condition in the country has not been created since we took office. It began years before that, under the dominion of the right hon. gentleman who said, "What have we been doing all along; just let it drift." We have heard something about parliamentary control being endangered in these times, and we have heard that this government wishes to take the control of matters out of the hands, of parliament. Hon. gentlemen should know something about what happens when control is not in the hands of parliament. One of the first actions of this government after it took office was to provide that our water rights, our navigation rights on the St. Lawrence system could no longer be given away by orders in council, but could be given away only by an act of parliament. Who was looking after the rights of parliament in those days, and who is now talking about looking after the rights of parliament?
I listened with great interest to the two hour speech delivered last night by the right hon. leader of the opposition. I used to think that the hon. member for Weyburn was a man of innocent mind. But I do not know of anybody who in thirty minutes could have conceived more means of being wicked in business, in the ways described by the hon. member, unless it would be his right hon. leader.
I heard the leader of the opposition make a criticism of this bill. He piled up some arguments, and then proceeded to knock them down. I heard mention of the Magna Charta, and that sort of thing. But let me say, Mr. Speaker, that when this parliament under the leadership of the right hon. leader of the opposition passed the Canadian wheat board bill in 1922, he did just exactly what he said in every sentence of his speech delivered last night was wrong, and should not have been done. There is not a single thing in this marketing bill, which the right hon. gentleman criticized last night, which is not contained in even worse form in the Canadian wheat board bill which hon. gentlemen opposite sat in their seats and voted for in 1922. Why is what they did in 1922 considered to be right and1 proper, and the same thing done at the present time considered to be wrong? What principle of Liberalism is it which says that what was done in 1922 by a Liberal government is all right, but that when a Conservative government does the same thing in 1934 it is all wrong? The only principle of Liberalism of which I know which admits that view was the principle defined by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) when he said:	" It is a principle
of Liberalism to have no principles." The principle of to-day is discarded to-morrow, and the principle of to-morrow is discarded next day. It is the principle of expediency. The party is operated like a weather vane. It tries to keep its ear to the ground, and stir the passions of the mob. When they succeed they come here and cheer. That is the true principle of Liberalism. Talk about giving authority to unnamed boards that you do not know anything about-that is exactly

what the Canadian wheat board bill did. Not only did it give authority to unnamed boards, but it gave authority to the governor in council to fix the salaries of the unnamed boards, and to fix them without consulting parliament. And Green's history?
Mr. TURNBUiLLL: They would turn over in their graves if they knew what hon. gentlemen opposite did in 1922 to the liberties of parliament. It is true that in 1922 the money that the government decided they were going to give to these gentlemen was not going to come out of the pockets of the general taxpayer. That is right. It was going to come out of the pockets of the farmers the hon. member for Weyburn has been talking about, and out of their pockets only. These gentlemen were not only regulating markets, but were put in charge of the markets. Having in their possession the money of the farmers they were authorized to dig into the farmers' money and to take out whatever the governor in council said they could take. But, of course, the liberties of parliament were not at stake at all-oh no.
The right hon. leader of the opposition criticized at great length that section of the bill wherein he said the board had power to create offences. I do not know whether he took any great objection to investigations. I may state, however, that the wheat board was authorized to make investigations, and to go up and down the country making examinations. It is suggested that because a board may do some investigating and find out whether or not in its opinion a price spread is excessive, they thereupon create an offence. They do no such thing. It is the act which creates the offence. It is the act which states that anybody who charges more than he should or maintains a spread greater than ought to be maintained is guilty of an offence and liable to indictment and fine. He has to be haled before the courts of this country. He has to stand his trial, the same as any other person would have to. And when he comes to trial the finding by the board can not be used as evidence. He has to be tried anew, and his case has to be proved, irrespective of the board. All the investigation accomplishes is to discover whether there is sufficient evidence upon which a man may be placed on trial. When he goes to trial it is then for the judge or jury, as the case may be, to say whether or not he shall be convicted. There is no

Marketing Act-Mr. Turnbull
creation of an offence at all. The right hon. gentleman seems to think that this board is going to have powers to make regulations, and that these regulations, are going to have the force of law. There is nothing new about that. The wheat board act provides that a board shall be set up with powers to make regulations. Read section 14 of that act and you will see what it provides, and when you talk about trying to get around the British North America Act by concurrent legislation with the provinces you will certainly find it there, and the hon. member for Weyburn voted for it, even though it was getting around the British North America Act and upsetting the constitution and disrupting confederation by concurrent legislation with the provinces.
