Yes, passed by a Liberal government in Saskatchewan, and this board that was going to be set up in Ottawa had power conferred upon it by the provincial government to make regulations, to create offences and to provide penalties for breaches of the regulations, and the then government just before the bill was passed had given the board, that they were going to appoint, capacity to receive, have, enjoy and exercise the powers and rights conferred upon it by the provincial government. That was the power conferred upon the board by the provincial government-the power to create offences, the power to enjoy and exercise the right to create offences. That was all conferred upon the board by the provincial government, and the board were authorized by the leader of the opposition and his friends on the other side of the house to create offences, pass regulations, fix penalties and legislate-a board with greater powers than the representatives of the people have.
The leader of the opposition fulminated for twenty minutes yesterday because we were going to set up a board with powers to legislate, and we the representatives of the people before we could legislate had to get the franchise of the electors, and be elected to this house. But here was this autocratic and bureaucratic government going to empower a board that had never been elected by the people to make regulations and pass laws for the people of this country. Was it not terrible? Yet he had authorized in 1922 a board not only to pass regulations approved of by the governor in council but to enjoy and exercise such further powers as might be conferred upon it by the legislature of any province, powers conferred by a government outside of this government altogether, and this board had the power to create offences and fix the penalties for them, and there was not a whimper from any hon. gentleman opposite at that time about the constitution or about the Bill of Rights or Magna Charta or any of these other great disturbing things that

Marketing Act-Mr. Turnbull
are going to upset all true and tried government in this country at the present time. I suppose that William and Mary never even heard of it.
The leader of the opposition referred yesterday to this unnamed board, appointed by governor in council, not by parliament, which was going to put into effect a scheme of operations not submitted to parliament, and with salaries fixed by governor in council, with allowances provided by the governor in council, and with all the powers which are being conferred upon them. Talk about a board for regulating trade; they were going to take the trade, according to the leader of the opposition. He talked about the poor fellow who could not sell his eggs and could not sell or export his butter and other articles. Why, Mr. Speaker, under this other act which I have cited if a single farmer in the province of Saskatchewan took a bushel of wheat and sold it to his neighbour for seed without the consent of the board he was liable to the penalty provided in the regulations that parliament had never approved of.
Now tell us about the bill that Anderson put through.

I am not talking about the bill Anderson put through. I will talk about the bill Pattullo put through, if you like.
This board that hon. gentlemen opposite were going to set up had power to go through this country and appoint agencies, companies and organization all over Canada, and nobody thought that the constitution was being overturned or that the liberty of the subject was in danger. Not only was that board unnamed but the government went up and down the country for six months trying to fill the positions on the board, and they could not get anybody to adopt the baby that had been left on the doorstep.
Some question was raised yesterday as to the marketing of wheat under the bill now before us. There is not a single thing in the four corners of the marketing bill that is not on the statute books of this country now so far as the marketing of wheat is concerned. The wheat board bill has never been repealed-[DOT]
Then why the bill?
-for purely political purposes.
We know it.

Did my hon. friend mean the marketing bill? Because as my hon. friend knows, the Canada Wheat Board Act

covered wheat and grain, but it did not cover my hon. friend's cattle nor his butter and eggs. We do not wish to take power to take a man's wheat from him and force him to deliver it or to sell it to us, and then transfer it again, but we want a certain amount of power to regulate the travel of the farmers' products to market. There is not going to be any question of interfering with the individual marketing of grain or butter or eggs.
Does my hon. friend suggest that this bill is but an extension of the wheat marketing act?
I should hope not. I think my hon. friend was very much in favour of the wheat act.
The hon. gentleman seemed to be making a comparison. [DOT]

The argument I am making is not at all that this legislation is the same as the Canada Wheat Board Act. If my hon. friend had been listening carefully he would know that the leader of the opposition yesterday,-and my hon. friend from Weyburn also did it to-day-read into this bill a great many things that were not in it and condemned those things. I have been pointing out that the very things that are not in this bill, and which the leader of the opposition condemned, were the very things he had enacted in 1922.
The object of this bill is entirely different from that of the wheat board act of 1922. There is no intention in this bill to take over the products of the producers of this country. The leader of the opposition went very far afield when he suggested that boots and shoes came within the purview of this bill, as well as furniture and a lot of other things. It simply indicated that he had not read the bill very carefully, if at all. If he had read it with any degree of care he would not have made those statements which he repeated over and over again, not simply once or twice, but three or four times, and which had absolutely no foundation so far as this bill is concerned.
This bill deals with the natural products which are mentioned and with other articles of food and drink that are made from those natural products, and unless my hon. friend turns to eating his boots, as he may have to do before he gets out of Prince Albert, this bill will not apply to him at all. The whole purpose of the bill is confined to those things which the leader of the opposition himself said were desirable. The sole and whole purpose of the bill is to provide for the orderly

23SL
Marketing Act-Mr. Turnbull
travel of goods to market with as little interference as possible with the actions of individuals in getting those goods to market. My hon. friends on the other side of the house, of both parties, have over and over again declared that to-day our problem is not one of production but of distribution-[DOT] that we were producing more goods than we could distribute. Now, this bill is an attempt to solve in some degree the problem of distribution ; it is an effort to assist in that direction. There is not a single thing in the bill about production being restricted.
Did you read it?
I did read it, and there is in it nothing that says that the government or the board may restrict production.
They will licence producers and through that may restrict anything.

Hon. gentlemen have
wandered far afield in their endeavour to find points to criticize. The most strained interpretations conceivable have been put upon the bill. Do not hon. gentlemen think that we should be serving our constituents better if, instead of trying to deal with the bill in the manner in which my hon. friends opposite have discussed it, they took the view that at least it is a step in the right direction? Let us approach the consideration of the bill from this point of view, that it is going to be put into force, and the machinery operated, by decent, sensible people who will endeavour to serve the interests of those whom they will be trying to serve. Let us take that view rather than proceed on the assumption that all the scoundrels and scalawags that can be got together will be put on the board for the sole purpose of hampering the administration of the legislation and making the whole thing impossible. Let us take a different view of the bill from that. Why not assume its success as a possibility if not a probability, and that it will be of assistance to those whom it is intended to help? I am one of those who would be in favour of the greatest freedom in the marketing of products, and I should say that every man ought to market his own products as best he can, if only we were moving into unrestricted markets. But the fact is that we are not moving into unrestricted markets; we are moving into markets where it is not possible for everyone to market his products.

How will this bill open
markets or remove restrictions?

No one suggests that
the bill is going to open markets or remove restrictions. That is one of the things which 74726-151 i
the hon. gentleman assumes that the bill is going to do and then he criticizes it because he says it is not going to do that. This bill was intended to enable the producer to get his products to market as best he may under the conditions that are prevailing in the restricted markets of the world, and to pro- ' vide that you do not throw five or ten million barrels of one product upon a market that can absorb only half a million. The intention is that goods shall be directed to those markets where they can be best absorbed. Take my hon. friend's illustration about the lean cattle. The farmers of Saskatchewan had lean cattle and, he said, the board would prohibit the selling of them. It will do nothing of the kind. What the board would do would be this. It would direct that those lean cattle be placed where they could be developed into fat cattle and sold to proper advantage. They would not allow lean cattle to go to the stockyards and depress the price of the whole product. Rather, they would direct that they be sent to the men who have feed, to the grazing field, where they could be properly fattened for the purpose of being marketed under proper conditions. Surely that is entirely different from looking at the bill with antagonism and hostility, regardless of what our constituents want. Should we not try to see in what way the proposed legislation can assist the producer, instead of straining every effort to suggest difficulties, with all the devilish ingenuity which my hon. friend from Weybum seems to possess.
There is in connection with this bill another point that seems to me to be of value. We are faced with the desire of agriculturists in France, in Italy, in Germany and in Great Britain, to have as large a part of their own markets as they can get, and there would be a feeling of hostility towards us if we tried to flood their markets and put them out of business. And that is only reasonable on their part. When the producers of Great Britain or of France are dealing with the individual traders and farmers in Canada, there is no possibility of getting together with a view to promoting mutual interests, but if we have a board in control of principal products in Canada, a regulating board, then that board can meet similar organizations in other countries and discuss matters of common concern in an endeavour to smooth out difficulties by cooperation, rather than by competition. My hon. friends opposite seem to be tired of the word cooperation nowadays, because they are not using it to the extent that they used to.
I am not one of those who believe in governmental interference with business; I am of the opinion that the less governments are in
23S2

Marketing Act-Mr. Turnbull
business the better it is for both business and government as a rule. But there are occasions when cherished theories do not square with the facts-Facts are stubborn chiels that wilna ding-and sometimes we must make our theories accommodate themselves to the facts. We are not dealing with normal markets or marketing conditions, and theories that are of general application often do not apply under exceptional . circumstances. For this reason, because I believe that the bill if properly applied, as I believe it will be applied, will assist in the orderly marketing of our goods, in the placing of our goods upon the best market, in the regulation of grades of goods that shall go to those markets, in providing that goods in an improper state shall not be marketed, and in doing various other things that will assist our producers-it is because I believe that the bill will accomplish these things that I support it, and in supporting it I think we are doing something for our constituents and for the country at large and particularly for those people who are engaged in the production of primary commodities. It is agreed, I think, that the producers of primary products are those most in need of assistance in this country at the present time. It is the feature of this depression, it is the feature of all depressions, that the prices of primary products fall further than do the prices of manufactured goods, perhaps because the producers of primary products are not so well organized as the other fellow. When you are returning from a depression to normal conditions, then the faster you can raise the prices of primary products in relation to manufactured products the sooner you will reach normalcy. And if this bill in any way, by regulating the flow of goods to the market-not restricting the amount that will go there

will help to obtain better prices for primary products, thereby restoring the producers of such commodities to a normal state, restoring their purchasing power, which has been sadly depleted, then I say that such a bill deserves our friendly criticism and the wholehearted support of the house and not the sort of sniping and backfiring that have come from the other side of the house in the last two days.

I have
followed with very considerable interest the speech of the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull). I should like to reply to some of the statements he has made, but unfortunately I am going to confine myself entirely to the principle of the bill. I listened very attentively to what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) said yesterday afternoon and evening and I did not

gather from his statements that he approved of the principle of the bill. If it was a fair inference from what he said that he approved of it, then I respectfully disagree with the leader of the opposition. I want to make it very plain at the outset, so that there shall be no misunderstanding, that I am opposed to the principle of the bill.
I listened also with interest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens); I am always interested in what he has to say in the house and I was a little shocked, I must confess, at his opening statement. Addressing the leader of the opposition, he used these words:
Did he recognize at all that there had been a complete dislocation of world trade?
The Minister of Trade and Commerce is in charge of the bureau of statistics and for the work I have to do I lean very much upon that bureau. I regard accuracy of statement as the first essential of the bureau of statistics and I expect that from the minister in charge. I have before me a statement as to the actual condition of world trade as published by the League of Nations. There has been dislocation; there has been shrinkage. I am quoting now from volume three for the present year. It will be found that there has been a shrinkage in prices on the present rates of exchange of something around 50 per cent. That is not a complete dislocation of trade. It will be found that there has been a shrinkage of some 25 per cent in volume, in quantum. In other words, let me make that statement very plain. On the present rates of exchange trade at the end of the period quoted was, in dollars, some 50 per cent of what it was at the commencement of the crisis in 1929 and some 75 per cent in quantum of what it was in 1929. That is not a complete dislocation of trade.
I want to-day, if I can, to fit this bill into the world condition of trade, into the system of trade. We have heard in this house much of nomenclature. Sometimes we say that a thing is socialistic and it depends upon who says it whether we condemn or approve it. I want to know just what this measure is and shall confine myself first of all to making an inquiry. In the first place the Minister of Trade and Commerce yesterday evening was, it seems t >
me, just a little bit unfair in suggesting that we on this side of the house were not greatly concerned over present conditions. I have been following them with great anxiety. I realize that the government and the economic and political institutions of this country were subjected to severe strain and I feared that they would crack under it.

Marketing Act-Mr. Moore (Ontario)
I may be wrong, but I see in this bill evidence that my fears are well grounded. I regard the bill as one of the most important, one of the most revolutionary measures that has ever been introduced into this house. Some reference has been made to its history and it may be that I can throw a little light upon that. I understood the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), to say that the bill had been copied from the Agricultural Marketing Act of Great Britain. In this house we are justifiably proud of copying British precedents, especially when they come from the United Kingdom.

I am afraid the
hon. member is making a slight misrepresentation of what I intended to convey.
I shall be glad to be corrected.
I said it did in part include some of the principles of the British marketing act.

I accept the correction. I would like to go a little bit further and refer to something that seems to me at any rate to cover more clearly the principles laid down in the bill. This is a statement taken from an Economic Survey of Australia, volume 158, published in November, 1931, and given by the lecturer on marketing, university of Melbourne, Australia. In this statement hon. members will notice where the word "scheme" is derived. The lecturer says:
In the inauguration of its agricultural organization scheme in 1922, the Queensland government provided what is perhaps the most remarkable instance of extreme legislative support of centralized marketing.
That bill was amended in 1929 and this is what the lecturer has to say of its character:
Under this act, the government may at any time notify its intention to provide for the controlled marketing of any commodity, but provision is made for a poll of producers of the commodity to be taken on the question, if such is demanded, in which case 60 per cent of the votes cast must be in favour of control. ... If the vote is favourable, or if no vote is demanded, a board authorized by the act to make all arrangements for the marketing of the whole of the product, is elected' by the producers of the commodity concerned, together with one representative of the government. The scheme is not one of government control, but one of "compulsory cooperation."
If that is not the father of the act, it is the grandfather. It seems to me that the two principles are the same. I can well recall some hon. members raising their eyebrows askance at that time and stating that
that was socialism; that the action of the Queensland government was socialistic. Well, if it was then, it still is; there is no doubt about that.
I want to go just a step further. There has been some protest in the house about reference to what King John did at Runnymede and the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) was criticized for quoting John Stuart Mill. I am going to bring the house up to date and make a quotation from Doctor Robert Liefmann, on Cartels Concerns and Trusts, printed in 1932. I presume hon. members will recognize that Doctor Liefmann is regarded as a world authority on the subject. He is professor at Freiburg university. He says at page 222:
The tendency towards compulsory organization of industry springs in part from socialistic ideals, since the socialists welcome anything which has the appearance of planned economy, and are quite willing to make use of capitalistic forms of organization to this end, as the syndicates and trusts of soviet Russia show. The expressions "socialism" and "socialization" have thus become extended to cover all sorts of organizations regulated by the state, in which, however, there is no question of the abolition of private property.
Now I take it that this government was not elected as a socialist government. That was not the platform on which they appealed to the country. We have had well recognized socialist views in Canada, presented by two parties. I shall be glad to be corrected if I am wrong in saying that the C.C.F. and the communist party have differed flatly on this ground: the C.C.F. have said, We want a mandate from the people to introduce socialism; the communist party are prepared to introduce it with or without a mandate. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to say in all fairness this government should have a mandate from the people before they effect such a violent change in the economic life of this country. Not a mandate such as has been suggested by the Natural Products Marketing Act; the vote of say 60 per cent of the producers, that would not satisfy me at all. I have not the slightest doubt that if you wens to put the question to the potato producers, "Will you have competition or not"? You would get about the same response as if you put it to the politicians , in respect to the next election. Probably the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) and myself, are the only two in the house who would vote for competition at the next election. And I am not so sure of myself.
The leader of the opposition last night did not visualize this bill quite as I would. He

Marketing Act-Mr. Moore (Ontario)
had an idea of a body of men sitting here while parliament was not in session. Now the bill-and I have no desire to go into its clauses in detail-you will find, establishes a corporate body. That is the usual phrase. I have visualized a corporative state. I have visualized an occupational parliament. They exist in other countries. It seems to me that you have here the charter of such a body sitting in Ottawa, with the civil service, with power of taxation, as has been pointed out, with certain powers over the tariff. I have visualized that this parliament will abdicate the most important economic function that it has to perform, namely holding the scales evenly between buyers and sellers. It turns over the scales to the massed strength of the producers to be used against the scattered weakness of the consumers. I have read very carefully the bill in its different clauses and I find clause after clause which says, Pay, pay, pay. The power is given to tax the producers themselves. But if the taxation ended there it would clearly be of no benefit to the producers, so I take it that the principle is, Pay and pass. That is a well recognized principle in relation to all marketing boards. In the marketing board of the United Kingdom, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) well knows the subject is now a matter of discussion. Take the wheat import board of the United Kingdom, the board that deals with the wheat produced locally. The Minister of Agriculture knows that there is what is called a processing tax. The miller collects it, he pays to the wheat growers of the United Kingdom a deficiency payment, the difference between the price actually received and the price that is fixed by the government. Now here is the criticism that applies at that point. What is the amount, what taxation does the consumer actually pay in connection with that act? The matter came before the British house the other day. Mr. Elliot was asked:	What was the
expense of the marketing board? He said, I do not know. Then he was asked if the request were put on the record would he be able to tell within a reasonable time? His answer was, No; the member ought to realize that the government has no direct connection with the board. Now those things have led to dissatisfaction. The marketing board in the United Kingdom is not wholly popular. It is a conscription of the housewife; how could it be otherwise than unpopular? This act will have less popularity in Great Britain. The people of Great Britain are going through a struggle, and we admire their heroism. They are ready to sacrifice for their own farmers and producers, but I

doubt if they are equally ready to sacrifice for ours. You cannot conscript the housewife in England much more. There are two million housewives in England on public relief. Even now there is a committee of the medical association examining the conditions of malnutrition in Great Britain, and the object of this bill clearly is to raise prices, and also clearly to raise them mainly at the expense of the British consumer. Mr. Speaker, this bill in my opinion-and I recognize the danger of prophecy-may have a very disastrous effect upon our imperial preference. I am going to give the government, and particularly the Prime Minister, credit for doing something that I did not believe could be done; that is induce the British government to put a tax on food. I must say that I still doubt the wisdom of it, but the Prime Minister and the government of the day secured the imposition of that tax.
They are going to pay for it later.

It is not altogether popular in England. This bill will make it less popular. The Minister of Finance will remember that during the Ottawa conference there were nine economists who considered the effect of a food tax in Great Britain. Their conclusions were published in a book called Tariff, the Case Examined, at page 140. I should like to read just a paragraph, and as I recall it this particular paragraph was written by Sir William Beveridge, who says:
Dominion farmers cannot, by any kind of preference in the English market, get more for their wheat than they can get without any preference at all, except on two suppositions: first, that they cease competing among themselves and form an export monopoly; second, that they use their monopoly power to sell more dearly to Britain than to foreign countries.
Then he goes on to say:
The second supposition is startling. If it ivere realized, it would mean that the dominions were using the preference in order to carry out a scheme of monopoly dumping from behind the British tariff at the expense of the British consumer. It would mean that the British people were being taxed in the worst possible *way to provide funds for subsidizing, not any of their own industries or interests, but either the dominion farmers or the trade competition of Britain or both.
Then Sir William goes on to say:
It is hard to believe that Mr. Bennett, before making his proposals in October. 1930. can have thought out their economic implications.
I find it very hard to believe that the Prime Minister and the government have thought

Marketing Act-Mr. Moore (Ontario)
out the implications of this act, because it seems to me-and if I am wrong I should be glad to be corrected-that it carries out the very fears that were expressed by those nine distinguished economists. It is bound to create resentment; .all foreign monopolies create resentment. Wherever you are subjected to the importation of goods upon a basis that does not subject itself to economic provision there is not only resentment but you render trade in your own country impossible.
I must say that I sympathized with this government when they shut out certain imports from Russia on that very ground.
I must say that I sympathized when it was proposed to raise the tariff against the United States on certain goods that were subjected to monopoly production, and I expect the people of England or any other country will have the same objection that we felt at that time. Australia realized the position. It will be recalled that at one time there was a compulsory marketing board for wheat in that country. In 1920 that board was dissolved, except in Queensland, for the very reason that I have offered, that it would lead to reprisals in the countries of importation.
I know the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture are familiar with the compulsory marketing board in Australia in regard to wool, known as "Bawra" the British-Australian Wool Recovery Act. That board was dissolved in 1924. Many efforts have been made to revive it; Sir John Higgins and others have pleaded with the wool growers, but the wool growers have said, "No, we must sell our wool in open competition," and it is sold in the open market. And I would have the minister recall that while wool has been and still is subject to some restrictions it is less restricted than any other basic commodity and has been the first to recover its price.
Denmark is in much the same position. I have not the latest information but I know that within the last two years they have had a free, open market in regard to butter, with the exception of the use of the words "Lur brand," as the Minister of Agriculture will recall. Ninety per cent of the butter made in Denmark is exported. They sell their bacon in open competition, and eighty-five per cent of their bacon is cooperatively produced. Some of it is cooperatively marketed, but the Danes said, as the hon. member for Weyburn echoed, "What we want is a market, and we want that market to be as free as possible. We want to encourage the middleman to go out and sell our goods."
Last night the leader of the opposition referred to the economics of scarcity. Well, all the information that we are being given today as to the reasons for this bill is old information. The Minister of Trade and Commerce pictured to us what would happen if we exceeded our quotas. I should be glad to have, from the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, examples of where we have actually exceeded our quotas, not vain fears but actual instances which would indicate a real need for this legislation. Otherwise I must look over the world, and I must say that schemes of this sort have failed. The Chadboume plan in regard to the compulsory marketing of sugar failed: it did not turn out to be the economics of scarcity. The plan was put into effect; in 1929 the visible world supply washover four million tons while in 1933 it was six million tons, and remember that the parties to the agreement kept their agreement, but there was a shrinkage in consumption. That is the invariable effect of the economics of scarcity 'and of marketing monopolies. In regard to coffee even the figures have been destroyed; twenty-seven million bags of coffee were destroyed. In connection with copper there was a marketing monopoly the world over, and there was a revolution in Chili. There was a revolution in Brazil in regard to the marketing monopoly of coffee, there was a revolution in Cuba in regard to the marketing monopoly of sugar, and we know that to-day Russia is another example.
I should like to speak for a moment or two about another feature of the bill, namely that having to do with spreads. May I say to the minister that I began life as a market reporter on Front street in Toronto. I knew those men who bought and sold the products affected by this bill. As I look back I realize that very few of the men I knew in those days are rich to-day; as a matter of fact I know of none. The proposal is to fix spreads. Well, a commission merchant may make one hundred per cent profit on a transaction and hon. members may say that is a very large spread. He may make one hundred and fifty per cent or two hundred per cent,-put it as large as you like. But the next day he is liable to lose as much on another transaction. How are you going to regulate his spreads? Is this the only legislation we are to have affecting spreads? Does the government for one moment think that it can stop with this legislation? I suggest that there are more inequitable spreads in wages. Is the government going to attempt to iron out those wage spreads? There are more inequitable spreads in wealth; is the government

going to adjust that? Once you roll a heavy burden half way down a hill it is very hard to hold it.
I believe I can see that the government have been following the advice of Sir Arthur Salter in a lecture delivered recently to Cambridge university. Sir Arthur Salter referred to legislation of the sort as a kind of bastard socialism pressed upon harassed governments by sectional organizations. Mind you, Sir Arthur was in favour of it, but on conditions. May I at this point read briefly from page 20 of his book The Framework of an Ordered Society:
X believe that we can both plan and preserve freedom on three conditions: That parliaments will delegate some of their functions to the executive, without abdicating their ultimate responsibility; that the executive will fit itself for its tasks by welcoming the assistance of those who direct the actual economic activities of the country; and that these in turn will assume the task of collectively controlling and planning their own activities, in association with government and through an appropriate organization.
It seems to me that is precisely what this government proposes doing. And here is Sir Arthur Salter's stipulation-and no inference is required, because he makes it very plain- that to carry it out you must have a world ordered economy. He puts it in this way:
The whole of these sectional planning and guiding authorities would be linked together by the formation of wider councils, drawing their membership by selection from the smaller councils, and culminating nationally in national economic councils, and internationally in a world economic council; these councils being suitably related to the governments, so that the whole system would' be an adjunct to-or rather an integral part of-the machine of government.
That is the edifice. There are two lions' dens, one in Moscow and one in Geneva. Canada would be unwise to go into either of them. We have a heritage here; we have a vast country, and we are proud of it. Every hon. member in the house is proud of it. Do you think for one moment that a world ordered society does not mean ordering from a world centre? And if you can order production you can order migrations, and we thereby surrender our autonomy. It may be that it is necessary, but I should like to have further information.
May I in conclusion quote another statement by Doctor Liefmann. Coming from a German, under present conditions the statement is of double interest. I can see reasons as outlined by the Minister of Trade and Commerce as to why this bill should be

passed. The hon. member for Regina asked us to think of these reasons and to give the bill sympathetic consideration. I want to point out-and I presume that is the purpose of an opposition-the difficulties and inescapable consequences, so that hon. members may weigh them. Doctor Liefmann says:
The resulting mixture of economics and polities, which keeps on attributing new tasks to the state, is a good deal to blame for the lack of patriotism so generally deplored in Germany and for generally admitted stagnation or even degradation of our political life; it has also had disastrous effects on our foreign policy. The state as the great defender of justice and welfare ought to stand above the economic system and work for social equilibrium within this system. If it is too much drawn into the war of interests, and has economic interests of its own all over the place, it loses its authority and becomes less and less capable of effecting the impartial regulation of economic life.
May I give that statement a home touch. I should like to quote something stated yesterday by the Minister of Trade and Commerce which gave me a picture of the difficulties that this government will face, once this bill has 'become law. I believe the minister did not mean what I have taken from his statement, but referring to apples he said:
For instance our friends in Nova Scotia, who are only five or six days distant from the British market can pour their apples in while British Columbia and Ontario might be handicapped in that regard. Or British Columbia might have say 10,000 cases going through by way of the Panama canal in cold storage; the market is in danger of being flooded, and someone from eastern Canada pours his apples in and destroys it. No one I am sure desires that.
Well, may I tell the Minister of Trade and Commerce if I were a Nova Scotia apple grower I would desire it. I would like to take advantage of my geographical situation, and I believe the apple growers of Nova Scotia, generally, will take the same position. In connection with this bill we are going to meet that situation over and over again because, remember, you have assigned all but the mineral kingdom to the new occupation of parliament, and you have done it because others have done it. If I were on the shores of the upper Niagara river and I saw a man plunging in, I would not follow him. There is scarcity and poverty on the shores of the upper Niagara but they are not to be escaped by plunging into the river. I would stay on land. If the situation is so serious that it means the destruction of capitalism in this country, and remember that our economic life is within a political frame, then I should

Marketing Act-Mr. Vallance
be one of the first to support this government in an effort to ward off what I at any rate believe would be the destruction not only of the social life but of the economic and political life that we have led and have been proud to lead in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I propose this afternoon to deal with the marketing bill before us from the standpoint of a wheat producer of western Canada. The hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull) gave to the house this afternoon an account of the different methods which have been adopted by the farmers of this country in past years for the marketing of their products, and he emphasized particularly the wheat board. Perhaps I cannot do better than give a summary of just what the farmers of western Canada have attempted to do in past years in the effort to solve this great problem of marketing the wheat crop of western Canada.
Their first concerted effort was to organize the United Grain Growers' Grain Company. That was the first, shall I say, cooperative effort on the part of the farmers to market at least a portion of the wheat crop of the three prairie provinces. Then came the Cooperative Elevator Company of the province of Saskatchewan. In the province of Alberta we had a similar organization. Then in 1919 came the wheat board. I know that my hon. friend from Regina was not dealing with the wheat board of 1919.

I was attempting
just before we proceeded to the Senate to enumerate various steps which the farmers of western Canada had taken in marketing the entire crop grown in the three western provinces, and I had reached the point where we had come down to the wheat board of 1919. I think there is a misunderstanding, not only in the minds of many members of this house but throughout the country, the impression being that when this bill comes into operation, if it does, it will have the same effect as the wheat board of 1919 had. So that when you take the legislation that was put through on both occasions to make it possible for those boards to function and compare that legislation with the legislation we are now considering, in my opinion you cannot make a just comparison.
I am one of those who believe that some assistance in some way is necessary to allow the wheat grower to carry on. I read a very interesting article published in the Farm and Ranch Review, which probably confirmed this opinion of mine more than anything else that has been drawn to my attention. This article appeared in the Farm and Ranch Review of December, 1933, and it indicates all the countries in which the government is in some way either subsidizing production or affording tariff protection. Apart from one

Yes.

No, I have no objection. It was a letter that appeared in the Glasgow Herald, and was sent to me by the Scottish Cooperative Wholesale Society. The letter is not signed, but it was sent to me from that society.
A most reputable organization; I am not questioning that.

I suppose it came to me because of the association I had with that organization in my boyhood.
In another communication that I have received from Glasgow, from the Scottish Millers' Association, eight points are brought out:
(1)	That the policy of Mr. Bennett and Mr. McFarland on Canadian wheat is wrong. They are holding the wheat at an artificial price compared with other world wheat.

(2)	That it may cost them very dear and reduce the consumption of Manitoban wheat permanently.
(3)	That it is not in accordance with the arrangements made at the Ottawa conference.
(4)	That it may alter the methods of baking so as to use less Manitoban flour.
(5)	That it is unfair to the importing trade to have a premium put on Canadian milled flour after their fighting a battle with the British government to get this flour in free.
(6)	That bakers cannot be compelled to buy flour regardless of its price, or a wheat regardless of its price compared with other competitive wheats.
(7)	That the Argentine is one of the many sources of danger because they are selling a very good wheat (64 lbs.) at 6/- per quarter less.
(8)	That the Canadian position with the Canadian farmers will be worse than ever.
The other night when the Minister of Trade and Commerce was putting through some of his estimates I drew to his attention the fact that these countries had been increasing their exports into the British market while ours were declining. He indicated at that time that as far as the Argentine was concerned the exchange was probably responsible. In regard to Australia he said the reason was the same. As to Russia, well of course there is nothing permanent there; Russia might at any time dump wheat in order to establish credits in any market. Then I pointed out to him that it was the "sound money" policy of this government that was responsible for our wheat not being sold to the same extent as in 1932, and coupled with that is the fact that the price of Canadian wheat was out of line with world prices. The letters I have had from the old country show that there was a time when they depended entirely on the western United States for their hard spring wheat, and if Canada continues to pursue the policies she has now adopted they probably will have to resort again to wheat from that country. The Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that the British market is the only potential market we have, in spite of the six cent preference. Now we propose to bring new legislation; we propose to bring in a bill to encourage the marketing of the wheat of Canada.
I have not time to deal with all the clauses to which I should like to refer, but before attempting to analyze the bill from the standpoint of the wheat grower I should like to say something about the wheat agreement, because it has to do with this very problem of marketing Canada's wheat. We entered into an agreement under which Canada was allotted a certain quota in the world market; this quota was to be passed down to the provinces, from .the provinces to the municipali-

Marketing Act-Mr. Vallance
ties and from the municipalities to the individual growers. I suppose the powers granted in connection with the wheat agreement will be passed on to the board to be set up in connection with the marketing of our wheat, because section 4 of the bill says:
The board shall, subject to the provisions of this act, have power-
(a) to regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated product that shall be marketed by any person at any time, and to prohibit the marketing of any of the regulated product of any grade or quality.
The average wheat grower in western Canada usually has his obligations fall due on November 1, and it is his ambition to sell his wheat before that date in order to meet those obligations. Even under the wheat agreement, without the application of this bill, it might not be possible for the producer to do so. I should like to recite a hypothetical case. We will assume that in normal times a farmer produces ten thousand bushels of wheat; under the agreement, whether it be the ten year volume and three year average or the three year average and three year volume, he will be given a specific amount of wheat to deliver. Under the ten year volume he will deliver seventeen bushels to the acre; under the three year volume he will deliver thirteen bushels to the acre. We will suppose that a farmer grows, as I have grown, thirty to forty-eight bushels to the acre; he is allowed to deliver seventeen bushels. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) knows, as well as it is known by those of us who understand the wheat industry from a practical standpoint, that if under the wheat agreement or under this bill I am permitted to deliver only a certain portion of my production, either seventeen or thirteen bushels to the acre as the case may be, and am compelled to hold back the remainder of my wheat, it will be impossible for me to finance my operation. How can the farmer finance the taking off of his wheat or the operation of his farm? If I am allowed to deliver only seventeen bushels to the acre it is financially impossible for me to pay the cost of producing anything from seventeen to forty-eight bushels. I am therefore not permitted to meet my obligations. The law says I am permitted to deliver only a certain volume of wheat, but it also says that I must pay my labour, my taxes, the grocer, the baker and all the other bills incidental to the operation of a farm. If this agreement into which Canada has entered is in the interests of the country as a whole, as I hope it is, then I say the wheat producers of western
Canada should not be asked to carry this load, because under present conditions western agriculture cannot stand it. I am one of those who favour the setting up of a marketing organization that will take delivery of all the wheat and then Canada can do what she chooses with it. We should not ask the grower to bear this burden; I do not think it is fair.
Coming now to the bill before the house, I find myself up against the same thing. The argument that has been advanced in connection with the wheat agreement, and that will be advanced in connection with this bill, is that the best place to store wheat is back on the farm. You cannot negotiate wheat when it is on the farm, Mr. Speaker; no farmer can go to the bank, in spite of section 88 of the Bank Act, and establish a line of credit on wheat lying in the granary. So how are we to carry on? I still say that if Canada wishes to control and regulate wheat she should take the responsibility of financing the whole operation, objectionable as that might be. Then subsection (c) of section 4 states:
to compensate any person for loss sustained by exporting, storing or withholding from the market any product pursuant to any determination or order of the board.
If the government suggest to me that I deliver only a certain portion of my wheat will they, because I have to store the remainder, pay me for the storage of that wheat? I doubt it. There are many sections of this bill with which time will not permit me to deal, but to which I have very strenuous objection. We come to subsection
(f):
to require any or all persons engaged in the production or marketing of the regulated product to register their names, addresses and occupations with the board-
What I object to most strenuously in this bill is the domination of a group, a board set up by order in council, with the producer never consulted and never considered. I believe in cooperation; I should be inclined to support a resolution which would provide, in connection with the growers of wheat or those concerned in the production of the other primary products of Canada, that when seventy-five per cent of the total had voiced their intention of so doing, the other twenty-five per cent should be compelled to cooperate so that the producers themselves would manage the sale of the product. One of the most regrettable features of the activities of the farmers in attempting to market their products has been the fact that they have depended upon men who, in many instances,

Marketing Act-Mr. Vallance
were not experienced in the marketing of those products, and as a result the farmers suffered. Under this legislation a board is to be appointed by the governor in council.
I would expect, at least, that the chairman of the board would be brought from the grain exchange in Winnipeg, because he would have a knowledge of the marketing of wheat. If my suggestion were adopted, however, and the farmers were allowed to band themselves together and choose their own board I think it would be much more efficient because of the interest they have in the marketing of their products.
Under this legislation we are to have three types of boards, beginning with the central board sitting here in Ottawa and including the provincial boards and the local boards. There is so much machinery involved in this proposal that it is enough to ruin it. I am absolutely opposed to this type of legislation. During the twenty-eight years I have lived in western Canada I have been pledged to the support of cooperative marketing, but in this act I see no vestige of cooperation.
Then we come to subsection 6 of section 4:
The board may require the local board to furnish full information from time to time relating to the production and marketing of the regulated product, and shall advise the local board in all matters relating to the exercise of its powers.
This subsection gives the power of regulating production. The board would have power to say to me how much wheat I may grow or how much I may market. First as an individual and a grower, and secondly as a representative of a rural constituency, I refuse to support any such legislation as this.
Then we come to the marketing schemes, and we find the following:
A representative number of persons engaged in the production and marketing or the production or marketing of a natural product

Not the producers. It may be a marketing organization. This subsection departs entirely from the rights of the producers.
[DOT]-may petition the governor in council to approve a scheme for the regulation of the marketing of such natural product by a local board under the supervision of the board.
(2)	The petition shall be filed with the minister and if he considers that the persons engaged' in the production or marketing of the natural product are sufficiently represented by the petitioners, the scheme shall be referred to the board with a request for a report on the expediency thereof.

(4)	Before any scheme is approved the governor in council shall be satisfied.

There has been a great deal of discussion as to the legality of certain pieces of legislation, and whether or not they are at variance with the British North America Act. I have before me an article from the Winnipeg Free Press headed Under the Dome, and dealing with section 121 of the British North America Act. That section is as follows:
All articles of the growth, produce or manufacture of any one of the provinces shall, from and after the union, be admitted free into each of the other provinces.
The point I should like to place before the government is this: Under the bill I am not permitted to sell wheat to anyone other than the marketing board. Yet the interpretation of the person who wrote this newspaper article, and it is my own as well, is that section 121 extends to the provinces the right to engage in interprovincial trade. Has this government to-day the power to tell me that I cannot deliver any of my wheat or the products of my farm to John Doe who may live in any of the other eight provinces? Under the bill now before me the government state that without their permission I cannot do that. First, I have to be a licensed grower; I have to have a licence even to grow it. Then I must be licensed to sell it, and can sell only to the board.
Or go to gaol.

Or suffer a penalty, yes. To me, Mr. Speaker, the penalties under this legislation are altogether out of proportion to the offences. I should expect that some member of the government would clear up the point I have raised in connection with section 121 of the British North America Act. As a resident of Saskatchewan I contend i have the right under that section to deliver any or all of my wheat to any individual who may live in one of the remaining eight provinces.
I am very sorry that I cannot support the measure, although I am in favour of a cooperative marketing bill which would permit the producers of any primary product to

Railway Act-Mr. Manion
attempt by joint effort to market their own products in their own manner. If this bill is so amended I shall give it every support, but in its present state I cannot. I have sent many copies of the bill out to the farming districts, and I believe when it is understood by those whom supposedly it is framed to help it will meet with the same opposition as that which it is meeting at the hands of the official opposition.
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

What is there to-day in
any law to prevent any group of producers from getting together for the purpose of marketing their own products?

No one knows better
than the minister that at one time an attempt was made to have one hundred per cent control in the three provinces. I am told by an hon. member sitting near me that at one time British Columbia attempted what the minister has suggested, and they were told that their action was ultra vires, and that there would have to be amendments to the British North America Act.

Of course that is not
what the hon. member said a minute ago.
What did I say?

I am not quibbling with
the hon. member; I was merely curious to know what he meant. The hon. member said that-

I would rather have
the minister ask me if I said it.
-he was in favour of groups of producers having the liberty to get together under a cooperative system for the purpose of marketing their goods. What is there to-day to prevent -them from doing that?

The trouble is that we cannot compel others to come in. I suggested that when seventy-five per cent of the growers interested in any one commodity desired that it should be made compulsory for the other twenty-five per cent to come in, it should be so. That is the point I made.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

The house resumed from Tuesday, April 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Reid for the second reading of Bill No. 21, to amend the Railway Act (rates on grain), and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Barber.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the other
evening my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. Reid) discussed very moderately but at some length the bill which is now before us, but as there was a good deal of discussion at that time I unfortunately did not have the opportunity of speaking for a few minutes to offer my views, and consequently the debate has gone over until this evening.
During the previous discussion one of the members on this side of the house moved an amendment in effect that the bill be referred to the board of railway commissioners, which after all is exactly where the matter should go to my mind because it deals entirely with freight rates, and if there is a more complicated question than freight rates that can be discussed anywhere I should like to know what it is. I presume we will all admit that the tariff, for instance, is a very complicated question, but to my mind it is child's play compared with the question of freight rates. I do not consider, sir, that this house or the government of this country or any government or any House of Commons previous to this one has been or is the proper body before which to bring such a question as this, with all due deference to my hon. friend's argument to the contrary.
The government of Canada in 1904 established the board of railway commissioners whose duty it is to deal with freight rates, and since that time, with one or two extraordinary exceptions, it has always been considered that the freight rate structure is a question too technical to be dealt with by this house. My hon. friend from New Westminster will not quite agree with that, but let me illustrate what I mean by that statement.
Let us imagine that this bill should become law. It would in effect make the freight rates westward exactly the same as the freight rates eastward on the basis of the Crowsnest pass rates and on the basis of the shorter haul from Calgary rather than the longer haul from Edmonton. That perhaps may not be very clear to those who have not looked into the question, but my hon. friend from
Railway Act-Mr. Manion

New Westminster and my hon. friend from Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) and others who have studied the matter will understand the statement. Now if you pass this bill and fix these rates at the present time, it does not matter what the details of the rates are; the fact remains that you are fixing freight rates in this house and any member of the house on either side and belonging to any party would then be justified in coming before the house and demanding that we also fix the freight rate on some particular commodity from his constituency moving to some other section of the country.
That is not a far-fetched illustration, because while my hon. friend from New Westminster was speaking the other evening I jotted down different products on which I have been approached this year by various members to your left, Mr. Speaker, and also to your right, in respect of which special freight rates were asked because of the distressful times in various sections of the country. I have had some hon. members from northern Ontario, for example, and some from southern Ontario take up the question of the rates on pulpwood, claiming that the freight rates are unfair to the pulpwood industry because of the low prices of all lines and the lesser demand for pulpwood and paper in the United States, and so on. My hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Veniot) nods his head in assent. He understands that question because he comes from a section where pulpwood and lumbering generally is a very important industry. On a number of occasions the members from this side of the house and from the other side have requested that the Canadian National Railways-they have even suggested that I intercede with the Canadian Pacific Railway-should endeavour to set special rates for their section of the country on pulpwood and lumber products in general. I have also had many requests from various parts of the country demanding special rates on agricultural products because of the very low prices that prevail at the present time and because of the difficult position in which the farmer finds himself to-day in trying to make ends meet. I have always answered that it was a matter over which I have no control, and I say frankly that I have passed these letters on to the particular railway concerned, the Canadian Pacific or the Canadian National, because I have no power to compel them to control or fix these rates. The only body aside from the railways themselves which has power to deal with the freight rate structure in this country is the board of railway commissioners, and I have pointed that out to

anyone who has approached me on questions such as this.
I mention that because it will illustrate to my hon. friend from New Westminster the Chinese puzzle which parliament would have to deal with if we attempted to enter into such a complicated question as freight rates, and to show the house how complicated the question is I am going to quote a paragraph from the general freight rates investigation made by the board of railway commissioners.
What date?
Unfortunately I have not the date, but I think it was in the year 1927. It is the report of the general freight rates investigation-
It was in 1927.
What is the special rate granted on feed grain last year?

I regret that I cannot give my hon. friend that information offhand. Personally I had a good deal to do with having that rate put into effect. There was held in my office a meeting of representatives of the different provinces who were here for the interprovincial conference a year and a half ago and I had representatives of the railways present. I hope I may be pardoned for boasting a little in saying that I had to take a club to the railways to get them to consent to it, because I had been arguing for it for a considerable time. Finally, after discussing

Railway Act-Mr. Manion

the matter with the representatives of the provinces, both railways conceded the rate. Speaking from memory, I think it is nearly midway between the domestic and the export rate-an hon. gentleman near me says it is 30 cents, and I think that is right. That rate they conceded after a good deal of argument and it is still in effect. They may wish to eliminate it later, but so far as I am concerned I do not think they should. I do not know that much freight has moved in consequence of that lower rate, but at any rate it was put into force.
Another point I wish to make is this. The rates on Canadian grain are the lowest rates in the world. That is the claim made by both railways and, I think, quite justifiably. They contend that the rates on grain in Canada are lower, by and large, than the rates on grain in the United States or in any other country over similar distances.
May I add, in regard to the amendment of my hon. friend from Fraser Valley, that I am entirely in accord with what it proposes, inasmuch as the board of railway commissioners is the proper body, appointed in 1904, to deal with this question. That board has rendered excellent service ever since that time, and I submit that this house would be most unwise if it undertook to become involved in this question. I suggest that the proper course is to support the amendment which has been proposed by the hon. member for Fraser Valley, on the principle that the board of railway commissioners is the logical body to which a question of this sort should be referred.

I wish to make just a few observations in reply to some of the statements made in this debate, particularly by the Minister of Rail-wa.ys (Mr. Manion). First, may I say that I am indeed pleased with the spirit in which so far the debate has been carried on, and in this regard I refer especially to the speech delivered by the Minister of Railways this evening. The hon. gentleman has quoted from the report of the board of railway commissioners in the general freight rates investigation, and if there is one reason more than another why I cannot accept the amendment it is the very paragraph which he read. If you will note the last sentence-and these are the views of the board in 1927-you will see from this statement that after all data has been placed before them, average mileage operated, the gross ton miles, net ton mileage, freight train mileage, etc., all of which are to some degree interrelated, not one of them

by itself leads to any absolute, certain and definite conclusion. AH this information has been laid before the board of railway commissioners many times but no results have accrued from the appeals made, some of them I am sorry to say very expensive.
I cannot agree with the Minister of Railways when he says that the settling of this question would be the settling of commodity rates. I would not attempt to bring into this house the general freight rates question; it is too complicated, as I am perfectly well aware. But parliament in 1925 changed the commodity rates of the Crowsnest within the territory from Calgary to Fort William and substituted therefor the Crowsnest Pass rates on grain and grain products within the whole area between these two points, settling definitely the status of grain and grain products. That is exactly what we are asking for.
As I have stated, our appeal before the board of railway commissioners has not met with any degree of success; it has been turned down time and again and it is in view of that I have endeavoured, since I have entered parliament, to place the matter before it. In 1925 they did not set commodity rates; they set a rate only on grain and grain products going easterly from Calgary or Edmonton to Fort William, and we in British Columbia are asking for equal treatment. We are not asking parliament to set commodity rates. Commodity rates do not enter into the question at all, because, if parliament were to adopt the bill now before the house, the only thing affected would be grain and grain products. The matter of commodity rates and the general freight rates structure is not touched upon and I will agree with some hon. members that when we come to that, those complicated questions should be discussed before the board of railway commissioners.
I am sorry I cannot accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber), because past experience has shown us that we can hope for very little before the railway board. As I have pointed out, the various commissioners who have sat in judgment have put it on record that the hands 'of British Columbia are tied, so to speak. They did not say so in so many words, but they said that the Crowsnest rate from Calgary to Fort William had no bearing on any appeal made by British Columbia as regards grain and grain products going west. The other evening I quoted the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) who took the attitude at that time that if parliament in its wisdom or otherwise had seen- fit to

Railway Act-Mr. Reid
change the act and give to the east those old rates, we should also receive the same rates westward. On that occasion of course, he declared that he would rather see the whole matter go before the board of railway commissioners. But inasmuch as the bill fixing those grain rates did go through parliament in 1925, my appeal now-and it has been practically the same since I have entered parliament-is that parliament should put into the act what was left out in 1925.
When the hon. member for Fraser Valley spoke, I am sorry he interjected that little remark about the anxiety I had and the delay in introducing the bill since I came here this year. It is said that those who live in glass houses should not throw stones, and it is equally true that those who have done little themselves should not attempt to criticize the efforts of others. It was due to that remark of the hon. member that I took the pains to search the records, and I find that in 1926 he was silent in regard to railway rates. In 1927 he was silent; in 1928 he spoke a matter of 103 words on the budget, and in 1930 he had a small paragraph. I would not have mentioned this, but I think it was very unfair on his part to cast it up to me that I had delayed this year because I had not seen fit to introduce the bill a little earlier in the session. That has no bearing on the matter, and I endeavoured in the course of my speech to keep away from recriminations.

I should like to correct the hon. gentleman. I was not silent. I went to the proper tribunal, the board of railway commissioners, on several occasions, where I thought I could get more action than I could in the House of Commons.

The hon. member may say that he went before the board, but we have been going there for years because the appeal of British Columbia goes back, so far as I know, to at least 1921, and that province has been appealing before the board every year without results from then to 1930.

The matter started long before that. I started it myself in 1912, so it is quite historic.
Mr. REIiD: Yes, but except in 1925 no strong attitude was taken in the house in connection with it.
I took it up repeatedly.

Oh, yes, there was. Before the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) entered parliament, the matter was before the house.
74726-152 J

And after.
Mr. REll): Now that the minister has entered into the argument, I wonder whether he would suggest to the government that they adopt the proposal he made in 1925. When the bill was before the house then, he said: "Abrogate the whole agreement". Would he now advise his government to abrogate the Crowsnest agreement as he suggested when he was arguing in 1925?
It was abrogated long ago by the government the hon. member supports.

That is another angle. It was not abrogated in the true sense of the word; ia was changed in 1925. It may have been abrogated by a decision of the board, but it was reinstated and the present legislation was put through the house in 1925. In that year the Minister of Trade and Commerce said that he was in favour of abrogating the whole thing. That is what he said then. Seeing that he has entered into the discussion, would he now advise the government to abrogate the Crowsnest agreement and leave the whole matter of grain and grain products to the board of railway commissioners?
May I interrupt my hon. friend? He seems to think he is making a statement that will embarrass me.
Oh, no.

It does not in the slightest. The first speech I made in the House of Commons in 1911, I made on this question, and I advocated the same principle as that enunciated by my colleague to-night, that the question of railway rate fixing ought to be in the hands of the railway board.

I think I am making a fair statement when I say that the minister gave it as his opinion in 1925 that seeing the Crowsnest pass agreement was being changed in that year and subsection 6 put into it, the hands of British Columbia were tied so far as going (before the railway board was concerned. That is the stand the minister has taken. He stated it three times in his speech and I agree with that. If he was correct then, would he take the same stand now?
This move for equalization of rates is a fight on the part of British Columbia and we have tried to bring it where redress should be given-to the foot of the throne. It is not a freight rates investigation or of settling the whole question of freight rates on goods passing between the prairies and British Columbia. We are asking for just what parliament gave to the eastern provinces in
Railway Act-Mr. Reid

1925; it is an appeal for equality and equality only. As I was pointing out, the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I are in agreement regarding the fact that it is useless to go before the board of railway commissioners since the act was passed in 1925, although it was a Liberal administration that had it passed, I am agreeing with him in his opinion that it tied the hands of British Columbia and subsequent events have proved that to be the case. I think that is pretty clear.
There are in British Columbia and, I suppose, in Alberta and also Saskatchewan, large quantities of low grade grain, and as our foreign markets are getting less we are wondering to-day where we shall find markets for that grain. There is in British Columbia a market and there would be a greater one if that grain could be moved there at a reasonable cost, but when those who would purchase the farmers' low priced grain, or grain that is frozen, or feed grain, had to pay forty-one and a half cents per one hundred pounds in freight-I realize there is an agreement in effect for the year-when they had to pay the full domestic rate there was not a great deal of that grain moved. Production of poultry and eggs in British Columbia has gone down and down, and the situation is bad enough just now with the many hundreds of poultry plants not doing anything. One thing affecting them which helped to put them out of business was the fact that grain was costing far too much. Not that the farmer was getting to much for his grain; the freight rate was eating up too much of the total cost. British Columbia in 1928 was producing 27,000,000 dozen eggs, but for 1932, the latest report I have,, the figure had dropped to 15,000,000 dozen. Not only that, but the consumption of eggs in Canada had also dropped. I quote these figures to show that there is a ready market in British Columbia for the low grade grains of the prairies and mill feed for dairymen, if only we could receive the same treatment as the eastern provinces have had and enjoyed for many years.
Might I refer to one remark of the Minister of Railways? He mentioned the mileage from Calgary to Fort William, and said that when grain reached Fort William it was practically in the centre of Canada; it had not reached the seaboard. While he was speaking I noted that from Calgary or Edmonton to Montreal, which is the port at the head of navigation, the distance is 2,239 miles, and grain is carried all that way for 53 cents per hundred pounds, while we in British Columbia were being charged 41icents for a distance of only 642 miles.
But the rate eastward that my hon. friend is giving is the export rate. There is a domestic rate that is considerably higher.

I am glad the minister drew
that to my attention, because the domestic rate as far as Montreal is concerned is some three cents per hundred pounds. It is only a paper rate; there is practically no domestic grain movement to Montreal.

Most of it is carried by
boat down the lakes, making a water competitive rate. Scarcely any grain is carried by rail to Montreal for export except a little in winter. Nearly all of it is carried in summer and by water.

That may be true, but the
fact remains that a rate exists between those points; 2,239 miles for 53 cents as against 41J cents for 642 miles.

But as my hon. friend
said, it is only a paper rate; it is not used.
If you take the rate to Fort William, 26 cents, it is much cheaper than for grain going west; and to Fort William there is no domestic rate.

There is practically no
domestic consumption at Fort William; there is only a comparatively small population. It is all for export, really.

Well I am not going to detain the house any longer, I am sorry to say I cannot accept the amendment, because past experience has shown us in British Columbia that we can expect very little from the board of railway commissioners. As is well known, we have appealed time and time again to that board and every kind and manner of objection has been raised as to why the same rates that apply east on grain and grain products cannot be given to British Columbia.
Amendment (Mr. Barber) agreed to on division.

International Boundary Commission-
Expenses connected with the maintenance in a state of effective demarkation of the international boundary, $27,000.

Will the minister give some explanation as to the progress being made in this work?

Supply-Interim

The work that is carried on by the international boundary commission in Canada is in accordance with the treaties entered into with the United States on February 4, 1925. The work consists of maintenance, which means reclearing of the boundary vistas through timbered areas traversed by the line, the keeping in repair of boundary monuments and reference monuments that mark the course of the line, erecting range marks to range the boundary over wide areas of water in the interests of the fishing industry, or to facilitate the enforcement of customs and immigration laws, and erecting new monuments where necessary to mark the boundary crossings of new highways, locating, establishing and marking the boundary on international bridges and in international tunnels; and performing all other related duties, such as furnishing to the several departments and bureaus of the two governments information relative to the international boundary.
What has been the total cost to Canada up to the present time? And has the minister any idea when this work might be completed?

The total expenditure up to December 13, 1933, on the field work of maintenance of the irteiyational boundary by the Canadian section under the treaty of February 14, 1925, is $67,428.09.
In regard to the second part of my hon. friend's question I would say that I expect this work will go on from year to year as long as there is a boundary line between the two countries-in other words, it will never be finished.

Has my hon. friend reference to a survey in the Northwest Territories, or any survey in the Yukon?
