I should like to ask the
minister for some information in connection with the Migratory Birds Convention Act. Some years ago an agreement was entered into with the United States authorities in connection with the sand-hill crane, which formerly existed in large numbers in western Canada and did considerable damage to the grain crops. The information given the settlers in Saskatchewan was to the effect that while these birds were protected in
Supply-Interior

Canada, when they got back to the United States they were slaughtered by thousands. I have no way of knowing whether or not that report was true, but that was common talk in western Canada. I should like to know if the minister has any information in that regard.

I have no specific information on this particular phase of the matter, but I may say to my hon. friend that I have met some of the members of the United States biological survey, and they are as keenly interested as we are in this country in protecting the migratory birds. Under the act we are required, as they are, to protect birds which fall within the provisions of the act, and I know that two years ago the federal government of the United States put into effect regulations which drastically curtailed not only the length of the season but also the number of birds that could be killed in the different parts of the country. I do not think I have any information in regard to the sand-hill crane, but it is certain that this is one of the classes of birds protected under the treaty. I can only make the general statement that to the best of my knowledge the United States are endeavouring to the best of their ability to carry out the provisions of the treaty.
When does the treaty expire, or for what length of time does the treaty remain in force?
I am informed, Mr. Chairman, that the treaty is for the period of one year and continues from year to year unless one year's notice is given by either party.
Does the minister say the treaty was for one year originally? I understood it was for a period of ten years.
The hon. member is correct; in the first instance it was ten years in regard to certain species of birds.

And then the treaty is renewed from year to year. If the treaty is to be renewed in the near future I suggest that the minister try to get some information as to whether the report is true that the birds are being slaughtered wholesale in certain sections of the United States while we in western Canada protect them. At times these birds come into the fields by hundreds and thousands, and it does not take them long to clean up a quarter section of grain. I have walked through a field where you could not find a kernel of grain left, just because of these birds.
Is my hon. friend speaking of the sand-hill crane?
Yes.
Is the existing treaty still between Great Britain and the United States or is it between Canada and the United States?
The treaty was made in the first instance between the government of Great Britain and the United States.
Then following the ten year period the treaty will be taken up by Canada, I suppose?
Yes.

Does the minister know
when the treaty expired? While he is looking up that information may I direct his attention to the fact that one reason for this treaty was to extend protection to mariners. That may seem odd, but still it was one of the reasons because of which this treaty was entered into. It is a well known fact to mariners that the gull often indicates a coming storm or a change in the weather, and for that reason the gull was included under the Migratory Birds Convention Act. The same statement applies to the wild goose, the brant, and so on. If we are protecting a bird under the present treaty because it goes from one country to the other, and it becomes a destructive bird in Canada, I should think if the government would take cognizance of what has been said by my hon. friend from Humboldt and lay the matter before the United States government it could be easily arranged to exclude that destructive bird from the classification of migratory birds. Of course, in making a treaty between Great Britain and the United States they considered the seafaring end of it almost entirely and did not think of this kind of bird as destructive on land. The gull, the brant, the wild goose and the duck are not very destructive, and if the United States could be convinced that the bird referred to is not a sea going bird but is a destructive bird on land, I do not think there would be any trouble. It is not like the similar bird we have in the maritime provinces, which is a sea going bird; this is a land bird, but it comes under the treaty. I think if the matter were properly placed before the government of the United States this bird could be excluded from the operation of this act.

Supply-Interior

I wish to amend an answer I gave to the hon. member for Humboldt a few moments ago in connection with the duration of the treaty. The clause dealing with that matter reads as follows:
It-
That is, the treaty-
-shall remain in force for fifteen years, and in the event of neither of the high contracting parties having given notification twelve months before the expiration of said period of fifteen years, of its intention of terminating its operation, the convention shall continue to remain in force for one year and so on from year to year.

The fifteen year period has
expired before this.

Yes; the treaty was entered into on August 16, 1916, and is now being
continued from year to year.

On a former occasion
when the estimates of the minister were before the committee I expressed my views in regard to this matter. I agree fully with the statements of the hon. member for Humboldt. I believe the hon. member for Gloucester makes only one mistake when he refers to the land birds and sea going birds, because I understood him to say that in his opinion a large number of the birds which went north from the Northumberland strait and the other waters bordering the province of Nova Scotia and his native province, New Brunswick, returned the same way.
No, I did not say that.

I must have been mistaken. The point I wish to make is this: Of, say, 1,000,000 birds which go north over the Atlantic coast or Northumberland strait not ten per cent come back that way. They come back through the prairies when the grain is ripe. They later go down through the United States, and finally reach Mexico. Not ten per cent of them come back the way they went up. They make a circular route, with the result that for years the Americans have enjoyed the advantage of this treaty; there is no doubt about that. Because of the fact that in recent seasons tens of thousands of those birds have been slaughtered, the eastern sportsmen of the United States are now taking steps in every way possible to prevent the people in the central and western parts of the United States from slaughtering the birds. They realize, as we do, that their people are getting ninety per cent of the advantage from the protection of these birds, and that in the
past they have contributed nothing whatevel towards their protection. It is high time that the treaty between the United States and Canada was revised.
Hear, hear.

It should have been
revised years ago. I hope the minister will realize the importance of the matter and see to it that we get a fair deal with our friends to the south which, up to the present date, we have not had.

Replying generally to the observations of the hon. member, may I say that the greatest known breeding ground for game birds, notably the wild duck, is in the southern portion of the Canadian prairie provinces. That fact has been established through observations extending over a period of years. While hon. members will realize that no definite or dogmatic statement can be made concerning the routes followed by birds in migration, nevertheless from the system of banding which has been adopted by certain governmental bodies and private individuals, and from a careful study of the banding practice, the flight of the birds can be ascertained with a reasonable degree of accuracy. If any hon. member will take the trouble to consult the charts which have been developed by the officers in charge of that work in the dominion parks branch he will observe that the birds which breed in western Canada follow many lines of travel when going to the south. A few weeks ago I spoke of the decrease that was taking place from year to year in the number of waterfowl in Canada. In spite of the treaty and of game regulations the fact is that during recent years the game have been decreasing to the extent of ten per cent per annum. I am advised by men who are closely in touch with the whole situation that probably the greatest single factor in the destruction of these waterfowl is the diminution in suitable water areas and breeding grounds. That is due probably not only to dry seasons but to the increasing cultivation, settlement and ploughing up of ground in the prairies-I am referring to that part of the country more particularly. As settlement extends, the breeding grounds diminish. The fact is that the breeding grounds are not all in Canada-and again I am speaking still of western Canada-but are international; so that when we come to consider the advisability of taking steps to preserve the wildfowl we must consider what can be done to preserve their breeding waters.

This will have to be on an international basis, and in my opinion the governments of the countries alone cannot do it; it must be done in cooperation with citizens and organizations who are particularly interested in this type of work .
I might also impress this thought upon hon. members, that the breeding grounds cannot maintain themselves; they can be maintained only by proper management, and unless there is an international arrangement between the governments, working in cooperation with voluntary sports organizations, taking over complete management of these breeding grounds, then only one result can be expected and that is the gradual but sure disappearance of our waterfowl.
In a booklet I have here which discusses the management of such breeding grounds, proper management is summarized under the following seven heads, which I think I might well read:
1.	Maintenance of water levels, as directed by engineers.
2.	Providing food and cover by earing for existing growths, introducing new varieties, preventing fires, eliminating grazing.
3.	Preventing trespassing.
4.	Controlling natural enemies where necessary.
5.	Practising sanitation to cheek disease and epidemics.
6.	Observing waterfowl and reporting concerning conditions, food, cover, etc.
7.	Attempting artificial aids in propagation where feasible.
Right here I think perhaps I should refer to the death of thousands upon thousands of waterfowl in western Canada during the past season. Moreover, it must be controlled by authorities with power to deal with the situation on an international basis.

I am not at all certain of the cause, but I suggest that due to the earthquake of 1929 a very considerable area of the bottom of the Atlantic off the Grand Banks of Newfoundland was thrown up, so much so that out of eleven transatlantic cables all but one were put out

of action, and it was found that the upheaval of the bottom had extended over more than three hundred miles. Nine cables were destroyed to the extent of about two hundred miles each. Whether that was so or not, the fact is that the disappearance of the eel grass synchronized with that earthquake. I am happy to say, from observation made in Pictou county, last fall, that the eel grass is coming back slowly. It will probably be five years before it gets back to where it was prior to 1930, but it is hoped that that will occur.

laboratories which carry on different operations, some in the Department of Agriculture and others in the Department of Mines. Then, of course, there is the national research council located here in Ottawa which carries on investigations into practically every phase of industrial activity, with the exception of the special work done by the laboratories I have mentioned.
Do research stations come under the same heading?

When we refer to research stations we have in mind research work carried on in the field in various areas. For instance, there is one at the Petawawa military reserve, one at Valcartier in Quebec and another one in New Brunswick in which investigatory work in the field is carried on in connection with the woods indigenous to that section of Canada. There is one in the Duck mountain area of Manitoba in which experimental work is carried on for the woods indigenous to the three prairie provinces, and we are endeavouring to establish one in British Columbia. That has not been brought into being, although we have officers who carry on these works on both privately and provincially owned lands.
How many men are connected with the research work in British Columbia, and how many are field men? I presume they are cooperating with the provincial forestry department?

Yes, they are. The personnel in the forestry laboratory in British Columbia consists of twelve officials, namely,
R.	M. Brown, R. S. Perry, E. Parr, Miss M. M. Harris, J. H. Jenkins, H. W. Eades, F. W. Guernsey, J. B. Alexander, J. T. Lee, D.
S.	Wright, W. W. Davidson, R. J. Eades. In addition toi these people we have a mechanical staff. In that staff are H. Chapman and A. White.
What steps have to be taken to have a research station established? Does the application have to go to the provincial forestry department or to the federal department?

If a research station is to be established under our administration the application should be sent to Ottawa. As I said a moment ago, in cooperation with the province of British Columbia we are endeavouring to establish one of these research stations, but to date we have not secured a suitable area.

The total seed collected

Section 8 of the agreement of the 20th February, 1930, between the dominion and the province of British Columbia on the transfer of the railway belt and Peace River block, provides for the appointment of two persons, one by the governor general in council and one by the lieutenant governor in council, to determine the location and boundaries of the several parcels of ordnance and admiralty lands within and without the railway belt. Are the relief camps situated in the national parks in Jasper and Banff only, or are they also in the smaller parks?
Relief camps have been established in Elk island park, at Jasper, Banff, the Big Bend highway, Waterton lakes, Prince Albert, and Riding Mountain park.
The number of men in the relief camps as of April 14, 1934, was 2,054, but at the peak of the season it was in the neighbourhood of 3,800.
How are these men employed?

They are employed on a sustenance basis; they are given their food and shelter and a sufficient amount of clothing to enable them to live in comfort and carry on their work. They are also given an allowance of twenty cents per day for the purpose of providing themselves with toilet articles such as toothbrushes, towels and soap, also tobacco.
Would it not be a good idea to have the committee of this house which is investigating low wages have referred to them the wages paid to these men in the camps?

These men are not paid wages; they are carried purely on a sustenance basis. They are given their food and the necessary clothing and fuel and shelter, and, as I have already explained, receive twenty cents a day, which is not given as a wage at all, but is given so that they can provide themselves with articles which otherwise would be given out on an issuance basis. May I repeat that wages are not paid to these men, nor has it ever been considered that they were employed on a wage basis.
Are they not performing some service for the government?
If the hon. member means, are they required to perform work in return for their sustenance, the answer is yes.
Are not the men in these camps working eight hours a day?
On days when it is suitable for the men to work they work eight hours a day.

And on days when the
weather is bad do they receive the twenty cents a day?

If the men do not work
owing to inclement weather they receive the usual sustenance and twenty cents a day.

To provide for expenses connected with the administration of Indian affairs, including salaries, supplies, relief, medical attendance, hospitalization, dwellings, agricultural activities, surveys, roads, bridges, irrigation, dyking, education, etc., and a grant of $100,000 approved by parliament in session of 1926-27, $3,939,500.
Mr. SMOKE.: I do not often take up the time of the house discussing matters that come before it, but I have on two or three occasions in the past dealt in a very casual way with the situation that exists on the Six Nations reserve in Ontario. In order to introduce the subject I may have to go into what, so far as this continent at any rate is concerned, is ancient history. The antiquarian is an anomaly in Canada; people are not interested. At the risk of being considered a bore I desire to recall some of our earlier history. Some of it may be tradition, but not all. There are some records which are indisputable.
I am not as young as I used to be, I remember well an incident which occurred during the Fenian raid in 1866. There are probably few in the house who can recall that raid; with the exception of our dear old friend the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black), whose absence from this chamber during the session we all regret, and our beloved friend the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White), I doubt whether there is another hon. member whose memory will serve to recall any of the incidents of the raid. My memory of it, while fragmentary, is distinct so far as it goes. I .remember my father and mother returning from town one day in their democrat wagon and telling us on their arrival home that the Fenians were over. I could take hon. members to within twenty feet of the very spot where I stood at the time. In saying that my youthfulness has gone, I am reminded of a saying which few in the house will remember but which I think was attributed to the late Sir John A Macdonald by either the Toronto Globe or our old friend the late J. W. Bengough. When Sir John made the remark that his youthfulness was gone, I believe that paper put it that his "usefulness" was gone. That may be so in my case.
I like, however, to reflect on those early days. My early reading of British and Canadian history brings back to my mind the pride which we felt in our treatment of the Indians as compared with that which they received in the United States. But let us reflect and see whether that pride can be justified and whether we have done all we could or should have done in justice to the Indians. I hope the Minister of the Interior,

Supply-Indian Affairs
who is Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, will take up with the Prime Minister and the other members of the council the matter to which I am going to refer. I trust, if he does not, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Public Works, who are both at present in their seats, will prod him along and see that he does it, because it is a very serious matter so far as our Canadian Indians are concerned.
Before 1492, when Columbus discovered America, the Indians were in sole possession of the continent. Whether the actual fact of possession meant ownership or not, Europe had no claim to ownership by what it was pleased to call the right of discovery, since the Indians were in possession, The European, however, claimed and used force to secure their claim, and, on the threat of force, not at all times by any means confined to threats, the Indians were induced to relinquish parts of America, their ancestral possessions, to Europe. In my office at home I have a photostatic copy of what purports to be a copy of an old deed, dated 1702 or thereabouts, some time during the first decade of the century, in the reign of Queen Anne. I am sorry I have not the document here to read, but I should be glad to furnish a copy of it to anyone who is sufficiently interested. It purports to be a deed from the Six Nations, or Iroquois, to Queen Anne, of a tract of land about 400 miles wide, and 600 or 800 miles long, which included, as far as I could make out the deed, the whole of the Niagara peninsula in Ontario and, in fact, all of old Ontario south of Georgian bay and most of what is now the state of Michigan. I do not recall what consideration is mentioned in the deed, but my recollection, so far as it goes, is that it was a pure gift to Queen Anne at that time because of the protection which she had given to the Six Nations Indians. This document appears to be the first link in the chain of title to that portion of our country.
During the revolutionary war in the United States, the Six Nations were allies of the British crown and fought side by side with the British armies against the armies of Washington, and, after the treaty of peace the Indians, like the Loyalists of British descent in New York state, lost their lands which were confiscated by the United States government. As compensation for such loss and in gratitude to the Indians for their great assistance in the revolutionary war, Governor Haldimand, acting on behalf of the British government, granted to the Six Nations a tract of land six miles wide on either side of the Grand river from its mouth to its source. This stretch of land twelve miles wide extended from lake 74726-1531
Erie nearly up to Georgian bay in what is now the county of Grey. The Indians accordingly migrated from New York state to that portion of Canada. I have no record of the numbers of Indians who took part in this migration. Their descendants number now, however, probably 5,000 souls and are confined to the township of Tuscarora in the county of Brant and the township of Oneida in the county of Haldimand. It might be asked: why are they confined to this small extent of territory? The answer is not difficult to give. The house should be reminded that the Six Nations Indians were the most civilized, according to our way of using that term, of all the bands of Indians on the American continent with, perhaps, the exception of Mexico, and they had taken to agriculture to some extent. Upon migrating to Canada this band of Indians took up agriculture to a much greater extent than they had done before. They had, while in New York state, been engaged very considerably in agriculture but had derived their living to a considerable extent through the chase and fishing. When they came to Canada they engaged in agriculture to a greater extent than before, and as the years went by were becoming less dependent on the practice of the chase and fishing.
This development among the Six Nations meant that they could not effectively and usefully occupy in agricultural pursuits all of the land in Canada granted to them by what is called the Haldimand treaty and they therefore negotiated from time to time sales of extensive tracts of their newly acquired territory. As patents, however, had never been given for the twelve mile stretch of land, the only way by which purchasers could be sure of the freehold of such land was by the Indians surrendering those tracts to the crown and requesting the crown to give patents to the purchasers. This was done. The purchase money was paid, not to the Indians but to the government then carrying on in Canada, and in the early days a very large sum of money was paid to the government as consideration for the respective blocks of land sold from time to time by the Indians, amounting in the aggregate, I have been told, to something in the neighbourhood of $1,000,000. Those moneys, which were paid to the government because the Indians were looked upon as wards of the government and not able to look after their own financial affairs, were to be invested and the interest received therefrom paid to the Indians to be applied to their maintenance from time to time.
Unfortunately, however, there were in those days, as there are to-day, promoters, and one
Supply-Indian Affairs

of the cleverest-and I am not saying that in a disparaging way-was a Mr. William Hamilton Merritt who conceived the idea of building a canal around the falls of Niagara-it developed later into what is known as the Welland canal-connecting the waters of lakes Erie and Ontario so that boats could pass to and fro. Mr. Merritt got a charter to build this canal. As a feeder for the canal, instead of taking the water directly from lake Erie, Mr. Merritt conceived the idea of tapping the waters of the Grand river some miles above its mouth so as to get sufficient waterfall to feed the canal, and he got a charter in the name of the Grand River Navigation Company. The building of the works of that company involved the acquisition of Indian rights from a point on the Grand river extending easterly to the eastern limit of their lands as given to them by the Haldimand treaty, and certain of the lands were taken, but without any compensation being paid therefor. Not satisfied with taking their lands without compensation, and money being very hard to get in those days, the happy idea struck Mr. Merritt of getting hold of some of the Indian moneys lying on deposit with the government as a result of the sales to which I have referred. The Hon. John Dunn was then receiver general of Canada, and it is said he was, if not president, one of the large shareholders in both the Welland canal and the Grand River Navigation Company. Therefore it became very convenient for Mr. Merritt to have a friend at court. Consequently a large sum of money was paid out of the funds of the Indians to the Grand River Navigation Company, and in lieu thereof the Indians were given stock in that company, a company which was never a financial success and out of which not one dollar was ever paid back to the shareholders. When I say this is a breach of trust I am sure my statement will not be disputed by any member of the committee, and I am sure it will not be by the finance minister, who is a good lawyer. I have not been able to look up the records to see when the kind of investments now required of trustees were defined by statute. It has been suggested that no such statute existed at the time these moneys were so applied. Whether that is so I know not, but even if not, the very fact that a subsequent legislature enacted laws restricting the character of investments that may be made of trust funds goes to show that what may have been considered proper investments a hundred years ago were really not proper investments; and even if in strict law there is no responsiblity upon the gov-[ Mr. Smoke.]
ernment, the rules of equity should override such strict construction, more particularly when, as I have said, the Indians were wards of the government and recognized as not being competent to manage their own affairs.
In order that we may have on record the figures in actual dollars of the loss to the Six Nation Indians by reason of the payment of this money out of the Indian funds, I give the following statement. While it may not be strictly accurate it is at least approximately correct. The transactions occurred when the currency of Canada was pounds, shillings and pence, but I give the corresponding figures in dollars:
Cash paid on stock in Grand River Navigation Company out of funds of Indians, $160,000.
Value in 1932 of 368.7 acres of land granted to the company without consideration at $40 per acre, $14,748.	.
Value of other lands granted' company in 1832 without consideration, 182.1 acres at $10 per acre, $1,821.
Lands permanently flooded by works of Welland canal amounting in 1837 to 1,826.8 acres at $20 per acre, $36,536.
Interest on these various sums at 4 per cent per annum, not compounded, $833,252.20-Total, $1,046,357.20.
The Six Nations are sometimes said to be a difficult people. I may be accused of being one who is seeking to make them more discontented. Surely the present Minister of the Interior, who as such is Superintendent General of Indian Affairs, and who, as I know, has devoted a great deal of his time to a careful study of this feature of Indian history and has familiarized himself with it, will not accuse me of seeking to stir up dissatisfaction. I know too that the Prime Minister, whose wide reading may possibly not have extended to this special part of the history of the Six Nations, will give this matter some consideration and do what can be done now to remedy a very great wrong. If this shall be the last appeal I shall ever make in this house, let it be said at least to my credit that my last words were an effort to redress a grievous moral wrong done to the Indians who were too weak to protect themselves.
The answer has frequently been given to me and to the Six Nations Indians that they have been recompensed for this money taken from them by the public works that have been done on their reserve. The government have been very kind; they built a splendid hospital, they built a school, they built roads; but that was done for other Indians also, and the Six Nations band should not be charged with this as against the money that has been misappropriated. Appeal after appeal has been made to successive governments in this

Supply-Indian Affairs
matter, but in vain. It is, however, never too late, and I trust this parliament will settle the question once and for all. Justice demands it, and until justice is done an injustice remains unremedied. A wrong is a wrong until righted. The longer it takes to right the wrong, the greater the wrong.
The plea has been made-I have heard it made-that the present government of Canada is not responsible for what was done by a government which existed before the days of what is called responsible government. I cannot agree with that plea. Whether the government that did the wrong was what is known as a responsible government or not, it was the actual government of the day, government de jure and de facto, and the present government cannot and will not hide itself behind any such plea. Or shall we say that the administration of real justice is a lost art? Previous governments have turned a deaf ear to the pleas of the Six Nations to correct this wrong. Let us return to the practice of our ancestors, now almost obsolete, of insisting on the righting of grievances before granting supply. I appeal to the government to go to the limit in undoing the wrong done to the Six Nations over one hundred years ago, and reestablish in the minds of our Indian wards the belief that justice is still the keystone of our national life.

I would like the minister
to explain what constitutes an Indian reserve and entitles the inhabitants to elect a chief. The reason I ask is that there is a reservation in the county of Gloucester, known, I think as the Gloucester county reservation, or by some other local name. The one who is recognized as chief of that reservation has had me write to the department several times claiming that he is the lawfully elected chief, and word comes back that that reservation is not entitled to a chief. I would like to know what the regulations are.

I feel certain that I
express the sentiments of the committee in saying that the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Smoke) has done himself great credit in putting before the committee the facts regarding the Six Nations Indians and their funds which were utilized over one hundred years ago in promoting the fortunes of the Grand River Navigation Company. I am not in a position to-night to enter into any argument, even if I considered myself competent to do so, upon this question which has now been agitating the minds of the Indians for over one hundred years. It will be noted that these moneys were, shall we
say, taken from the Indians, or to put it in another way the funds of the Indians were used by a government which was not a federal government. These moneys were invested, if my memory serves me correctly, by trustees who had been appointed by consent of the Indians for the administration of the fund. They, very unwisely as it now turns out, invested the funds in the Grand River Navigation Company, with the result that on the failure of the company the moneys were completely lost. Since then the Indians from time to time, both by representations made by themselves and through briefs put forward by legal gentlemen, have endeavoured to obtain the return of the funds which were so invested by the trustees in years gone by. They first made their appeal to the imperial authorities, as it was considered that the representative of the crown in the dominion had under his own particular control the welfare of the Indians. The imperial authorities did not see fit to recognize the claim, and then the dominion government were asked to reimburse the Indians for the moneys lost. The question was submitted to the Department of Justice, and in an opinion handed down by the then deputy Minister of Justice, Mr. Newcombe, he gave it as his opinion that the dominion government was not liable for these funds.
The hon. member for Brant, who has just spoken, has appealed to this parliament and said that in equity, if not in law, since these Indians are considered wards of the country the dominion government should reimburse them for the funds which were lost through the bad judgment, shall we say, of the trustees and those administering the province of Upper Canada in those days. This is a question, Mr. Chairman, which has given me a very great deal of thought. I am charged with the administration of the Department of Indian Affairs; these Indians are considered by practically everyone in Canada to be wards of the government, and we are the trustees of their estate and their funds. I think any man who has occupied the position of Superintendent General of Indian Affairs must be seized with his responsibility under those conditions. It is true, as the hon. member for Brant has stated, that on receiving the opinion from Mr. Newcombe to which I have just referred the department endeavoured, by way of works carried on in the reserve of the Six Nations and by the construction of the Lady Willingdon hospital, to liquidate the debt, if I may call it that. The hon. member for Brant to-night claims, as the Six Nations themselves claim, that this did not constitute a quid pro quo, that we carried
Supply-Indian Affairs

on similar works in other Indian reserves in Canada for the benefit of the Indians, and that they still want the return of their money. But may I say that the construction of this hospital and these other works were carried on for that express purpose. I would point out also that in some cases, and notably the Blackfoot reserve in southern Alberta, the reserve is practically self supporting. They carry on their own affairs and their expenses are paid from the funds of the band. In general I may say that this is the policy of the department; we endeavour to lead them in the direction of becoming self supporting.
I do not intend to extend my remarks in regard to this question at this time, Mr. Chairman, but I am very grateful to the hon. member for Brant for having placed the matter so clearly before the committee. I wish to assure him that so far as I am concerned, within the limits imposed upon me I shall endeavour to see that justice is done.

Does this vote
cover capital expenditure for buildings?
Yes, it covers all expenditures.

I was wondering
what were the chances this year of rebuilding the Indian school at Le Bret, which was burned some time ago. I believe there is some likelihood of a building program being initiated in the near future, and I do not know any better way to spend some of that money than in the construction of this school that is badly needed at that point. Le Bret is on the boundary between Melville and Qu'Appelle ridings, and my hon. friend knows the urgency of this matter. This was one of the early industrial schools; it was established away back in territorial days, and Le Bret is a very old and important settlement as well.
My hon. friend will not mind if I mention the none too good sanitary conditions that prevailed in the temporary quarters that were provided last year, though since that time substantial improvement has been made in the temporary quarters, for which I wish to express my appreciation. Even with these improved conditions, however, the minister knows quite well that the housing situation is not at all satisfactory. There is no doubt that this school will be rebuilt some time soon, and this coming summer would seem to be the appropriate time, if I might presume to make the suggestion. This is in a very public location; a railway runs right past the door, and this is one of the beauty spots of the Qu'Appelle valley. In addition to these

reasons we must consider the interests of the Indians, who are wards of the government and for whom the government as the guardian should provide proper quarters. It is true that the men were provided with excellent even palatial, quarters right at the outset after the fire in a seminary across the lake. The men always seem to be provided for first, among Indians as well as among white people. Everything was lovely so far as the men were concerned, but the girls were jammed like sardines into a frame building that was used formerly as a town hall.
I was a member of a government for many years and I know there is always the limitation of money. You cannot spend what you do not get, and these arei desperately trying times, but really I do not think those conditions, even with the improvement made last fall, should continue much longer, for the sake of the reputation of Canada. Since these Indians are the worthy wards of the country, as their host and guardian we should recognize the trust that has been imposed upon us and carry it out to the fullest extent possible consistent with the finances of the country. There does appear to be a little bit of improvement in our finances and outlook; I am willing to concede that and to express congratulations to all because of it. Times are a little better and they are going to improve even more I hope; the worst would seem to be- over. Undoubtedly the process of recovery will be slow, but these are interesting human beings placed in our care, and surely the government has a very strong obligation to take care of these wards and particularly the female members when the males are already so well looked after. The minister can only spend what he gets, I know, but I was wondering if a nice little nibble out of this large vote might be devoted to the worthy purpose to which I have referred.

A few moments ago the hon. member for Gloucester asked a question in regard to the system of electing chiefs on a certain reservation in the province of New Brunswick. I am unable to give a specific answer to his question at the present time, but I may say that chiefs are selected by two different systems. The first is the elective system, which is carried on under the principle of manhood franchise and which exists on some reserves in Canada, and the second is the old hereditary system which prevails on other reserves. I am unable to say whether on this reserve the hereditary or the elective system is in vogue, but I shall be glad to get the information and give it to the hon. member.

Supply-Indian Affairs
The hon. member for Melville raised the question of the rebuilding of the Le Bret Indian school which was burned in the fall of 1932. At that time provision was made, as he has stated, for the temporary accommodation of the pupils. The Roman Catholic church have a seminary a short distance from the site of the previous building in which they were enabled to house the male pupils. Manifestly it was not possible, owing to lack of space and for other reasons, to house the girls in that building, and temporary quarters were found for them in the town hall. After a time it was brought to my attention that the accommodation provided for the girls was very unsatisfactory, from every point of view, and we were able to secure other quarters. As the hon. member has stated, much better arrangements were made. May I say to him that I agree the quarters are not such as we would wish them to be, but like everyone else we have to cut our coat according to our cloth, and the arrangements which were made were only temporary in order that the education of these Indian boys and girls would not be interrupted. In our endeavour to attain that object we secured the hearty cooperation of the church authorities.
I recognize the importance of this school. It is among the first schools in Canada, was looked upon as the premier school of the Roman Catholic church in Canada, and one to which various church dignitaries were taken when paying visits to portions of western Canada. I am sorry to have to state that no provision is made in the vote before the house for the erection of this school. May I say to him however that I am hopeful, and I have a basis for my hope, that this Indian school may be built during the season of 1934-35.

I should like to bring a small matter to the attention of the minister. On the west coast of Vancouver Island there is an agency called the West Coast Indian Agency. It comprises some hundreds of reserves which, with few exceptions, are exposed to the full sweep of the Pacific ocean. For that reason it is difficult to reach them by anything other than a substantial boat. The ordinary means of travel to them is by a steamer which runs every ten days up and down again. I am familiar with the situation, because I used to be Indian agent and have often spent five or six days on the steamer to do only a couple of hours or half day's work. That is not an economical arrangement.
During the last ten or twelve years the department has maintained a stout launch which
was very suitable for the work, and afforded means for the officials to travel. It has done excellent work and through it good service has been done. Last year the engine in the launch played out, and after being coaxed to the limit of its capacity it had to be laid up.
I believe the launch was laid up in Vancouver in the early fall of last year. I asked the minister's department whether or not they were going to instal a new engine, and I was told there were no funds available. That was all right for last year, but when the new vote came into force this year I anticipated an engine would be installed and the work continued. However I was again told that no money has been voted for that purpose, meaning that the launch must lay up in Vancouver to decay while the work for which it is needed and required is not being carried out to the best advantage. That is not good economy. The officials will have to travel by steamer or by hired launches, an expensive way of travelling because even on short runs the rates charged are high; on a run of five or six days the expense would be considerable, and there would be very little economy. I would suggest that as the financial position has improved somewhat in the course of a few months it might be possible to get sufficient money to engine the boat and put it into commission again.

The hon. member has
drawn to the attention of the committee that this year we are not using the government boat for this service. That is correct. Upon investigation we found that about 87,000 would be required to put the boat into operating order, and on the advice of assistant commissioner Perry we chartered a launch to carry on that service during the present season. Therefore the official will be able to carry on the necessary work as has been done in the past. May I state frankly that this step was taken as a measure of economy, and to keep our estimates for this year, in these days of stress and strain, at as low a point as possible. We believe however that ample service will be provided through the chartering of the launch.
May I ask when the launch was chartered?
It is utilized as required.
When was it chartered?
When was that arrangement consummated?
I have not the exact date, but I can get it for the hon. member.

The point I wish to make is this: The minister has said a launch has been chartered to do the work. I want to know when the arrangement was made, because less than three weeks ago I wrote his deputy and renewed my request to have the engine put into commission. At that time I was told rather curtly that there was no money available, and that the boat would be left out of commission for the whole year. If substitute arrangements have been made to hire a launch I think it would have been only courteous and becoming an official writing a member of parliament to have given me that information. I want to know when the charter was consummated. I am beginning to think it has not been consummated.

I am sorry I cannot give the exact date that the arrangement was entered into. However as I explained a minute ago, I am informed we do not utilize the services of this launch continuously; in other words, the owner of the launch may use it for other purposes. An arrangement has been entered into with him whereby we may secure the launch at such times as we need it. Or, if it is considered advisable, the official may travel by regular steamship line. However some time during the winter of 1933-34 this arrangement was entered into, and again I must express my regret that I have not the exact information to give the hon. member.
May I ask the name of the boat, or from whom it is chartered?

Mr. Chairman, I regret I have not the full information before me. Lest I give the hon. member and the committee wrong information I should not like to go into a detailed discussion on the item, but should prefer to get the full particulars and give them to the hon. member. He could submit questions either verbally or on the order paper. I shall give him the information which is in the possession of the department or, in other words, the full and complete information in regard to this particular matter.

It really amounts to this, that no charter has been made and the officials must travel either by ordinary steamer or by hiring a launch, which latter is an expensive procedure. .
Progress reported.
